questions.question: In 1920 Ludwig von Mises published 'Economic Calculation in the Socialist Commonwealth.' His claim wasn't that socialism is inefficient — it was that socialism is IMPOSSIBLE. What did he say socialist planners couldn't have?
questions.answer: Market prices for capital goods — without private ownership, no exchange forms the prices needed to compare uses
choices: Market prices for capital goods — without private ownership, no exchange forms the prices needed to compare uses
A large enough computer — with enough processing power, planners could simulate every possible market outcome
Trained workers — socialism failed because Russian peasants lacked the engineering skills capitalism produces
Friendly trade partners — socialist nations could have succeeded if capitalist countries had not embargoed them
questions.context: Mises's 1920 essay sparked the 20th-century socialist calculation debate. Oskar Lange tried to answer with 'market socialism' in the 1930s; Mises and Hayek both rejected it as missing the point. Cross-link to history bank.

questions.question: A Soviet planner must decide whether a new railroad uses steel or aluminum. Both metals have other uses. In a market, prices compare them. Under socialism, all factories are state-owned — there are no market prices. What follows?
questions.answer: He must guess — there's no rational way to compare alternatives, so the choice becomes arbitrary or political
choices: He must guess — there's no rational way to compare alternatives, so the choice becomes arbitrary or political
He runs a survey — by polling factory managers, the planner gets the same information prices provide
He picks by date — Soviet planning manuals required ordering material choices by alphabetical sequence
He defers to engineers — technical specifications alone produce the correct allocation in a planned economy
questions.context: This is Mises's 1920 calculation argument made concrete. The planner can't say steel is 'more valuable' in railroads than in appliances when there are no prices to compare. Soviet planning produced chronic shortages and waste — exactly what Mises predicted.

questions.question: Oskar Lange in the 1930s proposed 'market socialism' — state-owned factories instructed to mimic market behavior. Mises and Hayek both rejected it. Why did Lange's answer miss Mises's 1920 point?
questions.answer: Without owners risking actual losses, simulated prices carry no real information — managers face no real consequence
choices: Without owners risking actual losses, simulated prices carry no real information — managers face no real consequence
Lange couldn't solve the math — modern computers can now run his equations and prove his model works perfectly
Lange used the wrong currency — gold-backed instead of fiat-backed socialism would have been calculable for him
Lange's plan applied only to agriculture — for industrial production his framework was widely and uncontroversially accepted
questions.context: Lange thought price-mimicry by managers could substitute for real markets. Mises noted managers without skin in the game face no real consequence. Hayek added that the knowledge required to mimic doesn't exist centrally. Soviet practice vindicated both.

questions.question: Mises argued in 1920 that socialism wasn't inefficient — it was impossible. Yet socialist economies existed for decades in the USSR and China. How is this NOT a refutation?
questions.answer: They survived by smuggling capitalist prices from abroad and tolerating black markets — pure socialism never operated
choices: They survived by smuggling capitalist prices from abroad and tolerating black markets — pure socialism never operated
Mises was simply wrong — Soviet GDP figures from the 1950s and 1970s proved planned economies could outperform markets
Mises meant the impossible was reaching the moon — daily-life production was always possible under planning instead
Mises retracted his argument in the 1950s after observing Soviet growth — he accepted that planning had worked in practice
questions.context: Soviet planners famously consulted Sears catalogs and Western commodity prices to set their own internal prices. Black markets handled goods the plan missed. 'Real existing socialism' borrowing price information from capitalism is consistent with Mises, not against him.

questions.question: In Mises's 1920 essay, the calculation problem applies specifically to capital goods (machines, factories) not consumer goods. Why does the impossibility sit precisely there?
questions.answer: Capital goods have many alternative uses — prices are needed to compare them, and prices need owners trading them
choices: Capital goods have many alternative uses — prices are needed to compare them, and prices need owners trading them
Capital goods are heavier than consumer goods — they require physical accounting planners cannot perform reliably
Capital goods are taxed differently — tax law was unsettled in the Bolshevik regime by the year of his publication
Capital goods include luxury items — and Mises objected to luxury on moral grounds in his published economic writings
questions.context: Mises specifically targets PRODUCER goods. A loaf of bread has one obvious use. A ton of steel can go a thousand places. Comparing those uses requires bidding between owners, which requires private property. This precision is why the argument resists easy answers.

questions.question: The 20th century ran an enormous natural experiment on Mises's 1920 prediction. USSR, China, Khmer Rouge Cambodia, North Korea, Cuba all tried central planning. The Black Book of Communism (1997) tallies the cost. What does the ledger show?
questions.answer: Roughly 65 to 100 million deaths — famine, gulag, and political violence, vindicating Mises's calculation prediction
choices: Roughly 65 to 100 million deaths — famine, gulag, and political violence, vindicating Mises's calculation prediction
Roughly half a million deaths total — mostly from World War II rather than from socialism's economic policies
Roughly two thousand deaths over the century — mostly from gulag prisoners trying to escape, not execution
Roughly zero deaths attributable to socialism — Black Book numbers have all been retracted by modern historians
questions.context: Courtois et al. (1997) compiled figures from regime archives opened after 1991. USSR ~20M (gulag + Holodomor), China ~65M (Great Leap famine + Cultural Revolution), Cambodia ~2M (Khmer Rouge, ~25% of population). Cross-link to history bank.

questions.question: Mises's 1920 paper opened the 'socialist calculation debate' — a 60-year argument across the journals. By 1989, who had won, in the judgment of even socialist economists like Harvard's Robert Heilbroner?
questions.answer: Mises and Hayek — Heilbroner's January 1989 New Yorker essay said 'Ludwig von Mises was right' about calculation
choices: Mises and Hayek — Heilbroner's January 1989 New Yorker essay said 'Ludwig von Mises was right' about calculation
Lange and Lerner — modern textbooks now treat market socialism as the successful answer to the 1920 challenge
Marx and Engels — original Marxist theory was vindicated when the USSR met its 1980s production targets fully
Keynes and Galbraith — the postwar mixed-economy consensus showed planning could be merged with markets
questions.context: Robert Heilbroner, lifelong socialist and Harvard economist, wrote in 'The Triumph of Capitalism' (The New Yorker, Jan 23 1989): 'Mises was right.' He acknowledged the calculation debate was over even before the Berlin Wall fell that November.

questions.question: In Mises's 1920 argument, the breakdown of socialist calculation happens not at any individual factory but at the system level. What specifically can't be done?
questions.answer: Comparing alternative uses of resources across the economy — local managers can't see what their inputs are worth elsewhere
choices: Comparing alternative uses of resources across the economy — local managers can't see what their inputs are worth elsewhere
Adding up factory output — Soviet engineers struggled to count units of production above several thousand a year
Paying workers correctly — without prices the wage schedule could not be set for any planned economy at all
Choosing colors for products — the absence of paint prices made packaging design difficult for the planners
questions.context: Mises emphasizes the SYSTEM-WIDE coordination problem. One factory can muddle through. The whole interlocking structure of capital — where each producer's output is another's input — collapses without prices to ratio the trades.

questions.question: Friedrich Hayek's 1945 American Economic Review paper 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' is among the most-cited essays in economics. Hayek argued the basic economic problem isn't what most economists assumed. What had they gotten wrong?
questions.answer: They treated it as allocating known resources — Hayek showed the real problem is using knowledge no individual possesses
choices: They treated it as allocating known resources — Hayek showed the real problem is using knowledge no individual possesses
They focused on consumer demand — Hayek argued only producer behavior actually matters in any modern economy
They emphasized money supply — Hayek thought monetary aggregates were irrelevant to allocation problems entirely
They overstated trade gains — Hayek showed international exchange was a minor part of any nation's prosperity
questions.context: Hayek's twin contributions in 1944-45 (Road to Serfdom + Use of Knowledge in Society) reframed the economic problem from optimization to coordination under dispersed information. The textbook framing — allocating given resources — concedes the planner's premise.

questions.question: Hayek's 1945 paper describes market knowledge as 'dispersed, tacit, and local.' A tin-miner knows his shaft; a copper-buyer knows his plant's demand. Nobody knows the whole picture. Yet metal prices coordinate millions of decisions. How?
questions.answer: The price system aggregates local knowledge into a signal — each actor responds without needing to know why it moved
choices: The price system aggregates local knowledge into a signal — each actor responds without needing to know why it moved
Central banks gather production reports from every facility — and broadcast a unified daily price across the network
Companies share data through a committee — meeting quarterly to align prices across industries that overlap
Government statisticians publish weekly tables — showing each commodity's correct value to the national economy
questions.context: This is the canonical Hayekian example. A tin shortage anywhere raises tin's price everywhere; users worldwide economize, substitute, or seek alternatives — without anyone having to be told what changed. Hayek called the price system 'a marvel.'

questions.question: Hayek 1945 distinguishes 'knowledge of the particular circumstances of time and place' from 'scientific knowledge.' A central planner can have all the scientific knowledge. Why is he still unable to plan an economy?
questions.answer: He lacks the local tacit ever-changing facts on the ground — knowledge that doesn't survive being centralized in a report
choices: He lacks the local tacit ever-changing facts on the ground — knowledge that doesn't survive being centralized in a report
He cannot make decisions quickly enough — even modern central planners take several months to issue any economic order
He cannot recruit competent staff — government economic agencies fail to attract talented graduates in any country
He cannot publish his findings — central planning agencies in practice never share their internal economic reports
questions.context: Hayek's distinction is the key move. The scientist knows general laws. The shipper knows this particular dock is short of crates this week. The plant manager knows his machinery needs maintenance now. None of that survives compression into a planning document.

questions.question: Hayek's 1945 paper opens by asking 'what is the problem we wish to solve when we try to construct a rational economic order?' The way the question is framed already prejudges the answer. What was the prejudice Hayek exposed?
questions.answer: Framing it as 'constructing' assumes a single mind doing the building — but no such mind has the required knowledge
choices: Framing it as 'constructing' assumes a single mind doing the building — but no such mind has the required knowledge
Framing it as 'rational' assumes humans are perfectly logical — but Hayek thought emotion drives most market decisions
Framing it as 'economic' excludes social factors — which Hayek argued were the actual driver of prosperity in nations
Framing it as 'order' presupposes hierarchy — but Hayek favored egalitarian outcomes through direct redistribution programs
questions.context: Hayek's larger point: spontaneous order emerges from millions of independent actors using local knowledge. The image of someone 'constructing' the economic order is itself the conceptual error. Markets aren't designed; they're discovered.

questions.question: Hayek 1945 was a direct response to Oskar Lange's 'market socialism' faction — they thought socialist planners could mimic markets by running equations. Why did Hayek say the answer missed the problem entirely?
questions.answer: The data the equations need — what every actor knows locally — doesn't exist in collectible form for the planner to use
choices: The data the equations need — what every actor knows locally — doesn't exist in collectible form for the planner to use
The math was too complex for 1940s computers — but newer mainframes can now solve Lange's equations in real time
Lange assumed honesty among managers — but in practice Soviet plant managers always lied on their progress reports
Lange wrote in Polish — and translation errors in his 1936 English paper distorted his proposed model substance
questions.context: Hayek shows the failure isn't computational. Even with a perfect computer and a perfect equation, you still need the inputs — and the inputs are the tacit local knowledge nobody can write down. This is the epistemic, not technical, failure of central planning.

questions.question: Hayek's 1945 essay calls the price system 'a marvel' — coordinating billions of decisions without explicit central direction. What broader political conclusion does he draw?
questions.answer: Markets are an information system — replacing them with central direction destroys the information, regardless of intent
choices: Markets are an information system — replacing them with central direction destroys the information, regardless of intent
Markets are perfect optimization engines — any intervention by government produces immediate and total economic collapse
Markets are inferior to expert committees — only academic economists are qualified to oversee resource allocation correctly
Markets reflect natural law — their outcomes are morally just by construction and never require any humanitarian response
questions.context: Hayek's conclusion is specifically epistemic, not ideological. The argument doesn't depend on planners being lazy, stupid, or malicious. It applies even to ideal planners with the best intentions: the information they need doesn't exist centrally.

questions.question: Hayek's 1945 paper was written during WWII — when Western economies had become heavily centralized for wartime production. What was Hayek's worry about extending wartime methods into peacetime?
questions.answer: Wartime planning works on a narrow goal everyone agrees on — peacetime planning has no such consensus, exposing the knowledge gap
choices: Wartime planning works on a narrow goal everyone agrees on — peacetime planning has no such consensus, exposing the knowledge gap
Wartime planning is too expensive to maintain — but Hayek otherwise supported continued central direction of industry
Wartime planning depended on military discipline — and Hayek wanted to extend conscription into peacetime management
Wartime planning had failed by 1945 — so Hayek argued for an immediate return to the prewar laissez-faire arrangement
questions.context: Hayek 1945 and Road to Serfdom 1944 came out a year apart — both warning that wartime habits would carry into peacetime planning and produce political costs as well as the economic ones. Postwar Britain and continental Europe largely ignored him.

questions.question: Hayek's 1974 Nobel was shared with Gunnar Myrdal, a Swedish socialist. In his Nobel lecture 'The Pretence of Knowledge,' Hayek warned economists against what specific error?
questions.answer: Imitating natural sciences by pretending to measure what can't be measured — then using the pretense to justify intervention
choices: Imitating natural sciences by pretending to measure what can't be measured — then using the pretense to justify intervention
Citing too many old economists in their papers — Hayek argued literature should focus exclusively on current data sets
Refusing to publish negative results — Hayek wanted journals to require all empirical findings to be reported quarterly
Building too many computers — Hayek thought economic departments should rely on hand-calculated econometric tables
questions.context: Hayek's 1974 Nobel lecture attacked the scientism of postwar economics — its imitation of physics in form without the data-controlled experiments that physics actually has. The complaint anticipated the modern replication crisis in social science.

questions.question: Austrian Business Cycle Theory says boom-bust cycles are caused by central banks pushing interest rates below the natural rate. From June 2003 to June 2004, the Federal Reserve held the fed funds rate at 1%. What did ABCT predict?
questions.answer: An artificial credit boom in long-horizon assets — most clearly housing — followed by an inevitable bust when rates rose
choices: An artificial credit boom in long-horizon assets — most clearly housing — followed by an inevitable bust when rates rose
Sustained non-inflationary growth — ultra-low rates would permanently raise the economy's productive capacity nationwide
Deflation in consumer prices — low rates would drive savings up and depress prices for the indefinite future of the economy
Equal effect across all sectors — monetary policy is neutral and affects every industry by identical percentage points
questions.context: Mises 1912 and Hayek 1931 had laid out ABCT. Peter Schiff, Ron Paul, and Mark Thornton publicly warned of the housing bubble in 2004-2006 using ABCT. The mainstream profession overwhelmingly missed it; the Austrians called it.

questions.question: US housing prices peaked in mid-2006 and then fell. By March 2008, Bear Stearns was sold for $2 a share in a Fed-arranged rescue. Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy on September 15, 2008. What does ABCT call this sequence?
questions.answer: The inevitable correction — malinvestments made during artificial credit expansion must liquidate when rates normalize
choices: The inevitable correction — malinvestments made during artificial credit expansion must liquidate when rates normalize
Animal spirits — Keynes's term for sudden mood shifts among investors that have no underlying monetary cause
Random shock — the Black Swan thesis says crises like 2008 are unpredictable surprises with no theoretical signature
Coordination failure — game-theory models attribute crashes to mis-coordinated expectations among rational actors
questions.context: Bear Stearns sale: March 16, 2008 (JPMorgan, $2/share, later raised to $10). Lehman bankruptcy: Sept 15, 2008, $639B in assets. The bust pattern — long-horizon assets falling first, then financial firms holding them — matches ABCT precisely.

questions.question: Peter Schiff appeared on Fox Business in 2006-2007 warning of a housing bust, mortgage securities collapse, and Fed-created crisis. Other guests laughed. By late 2008 his predictions had landed. What framework was Schiff using?
questions.answer: Austrian Business Cycle Theory — applied to Greenspan's 2003-04 rate cuts and the housing credit boom that followed
choices: Austrian Business Cycle Theory — applied to Greenspan's 2003-04 rate cuts and the housing credit boom that followed
Modern Monetary Theory — which predicted the 2008 crisis through analysis of federal government deficit spending
Behavioral economics — based on observed irrationality in mortgage applicants during the housing boom years
New Keynesian models — which had forecast the 2008 crisis using detailed simulations of mortgage default rates
questions.context: 'Peter Schiff Was Right' compilation videos went viral after 2008. He applied ABCT publicly. Mainstream economists in the same period — Bernanke, Greenspan, Krugman — overwhelmingly missed the crisis, with some explicitly denying a housing bubble existed in 2005-2006.

questions.question: Hayek's 1931 book 'Prices and Production' — the canonical statement of ABCT — argues that artificially low rates distort not just the AMOUNT but the SHAPE of investment. Where does the distortion show up?
questions.answer: In the time-structure — too much goes to long-horizon projects that only look profitable when rates stay artificially low
choices: In the time-structure — too much goes to long-horizon projects that only look profitable when rates stay artificially low
In the labor mix — too much hiring goes to skilled workers when central banks lower interest rates significantly
In the geography — too much investment goes to coastal cities and not enough to interior agricultural regions
In the size of firms — only multinational corporations expand during artificial credit booms in modern economies
questions.context: Hayek 1931 emphasizes the time-structure of production. Cheap credit makes long-term projects (housing, capital-intensive industry, R&D) look more profitable than they really are. When rates normalize, those projects look like losers. The 2006-2008 pattern.

questions.question: Mises's 1912 'Theory of Money and Credit' first sketched ABCT. Hayek expanded it in 1931. Their argument was that boom-bust cycles aren't inherent to capitalism. What did they say causes the cycle?
questions.answer: Central bank credit expansion — without manipulated rates, no systematic mechanism produces boom-bust cycles
choices: Central bank credit expansion — without manipulated rates, no systematic mechanism produces boom-bust cycles
Investor psychology — animal spirits inevitably produce cycles regardless of any monetary policy stance taken
Productivity shocks — random changes in technology cause cycles that no monetary regime can prevent or smooth
Trade imbalances — booms and busts result from current account surpluses and deficits between trading nations
questions.context: The Austrian counter-claim to mainstream cycle theories. Cycles aren't a feature of free markets — they're the artifact of central-bank credit creation that pushes rates below what borrowers would willingly pay savers. End the manipulation, end the cycle.

questions.question: ABCT predicts that during the boom, capital flows into long-horizon, rate-sensitive sectors. In the 2003-2006 US boom, which sector experienced exactly this pattern, while mainstream forecasters insisted nothing was unusual?
questions.answer: Residential housing — homebuilding ran years above trend, prices doubled in many markets, mortgage debt exploded
choices: Residential housing — homebuilding ran years above trend, prices doubled in many markets, mortgage debt exploded
Manufacturing equipment — factories overbuilt productive capacity across Rust Belt cities throughout that period
Agricultural land — Midwest farm prices rose sharply on cheap credit during those years across the Plains states
Commercial real estate — shopping mall construction in suburban areas was the primary credit-fueled investment
questions.context: Housing was the clearest example. Case-Shiller national home-price index roughly doubled 2000-2006. Subprime mortgages, no-doc loans, mortgage-backed securities — all built on the assumption that the Fed-cheap-credit era would continue.

questions.question: After Lehman's Sept 2008 bankruptcy, the US launched the $700B TARP and Quantitative Easing. The Fed's balance sheet went from ~$900B to over $4T by 2014. From an Austrian perspective, what did this response do?
questions.answer: It re-flated the bubble — preventing the cleansing liquidation ABCT says is required to restore sound investment patterns
choices: It re-flated the bubble — preventing the cleansing liquidation ABCT says is required to restore sound investment patterns
It successfully ended the crisis — the rapid Fed response in 2008-09 fully resolved the underlying monetary distortions
It produced sound recovery — by 2010 the US economy had reached fully sustainable post-crisis growth without side effects
It had no effect — Federal Reserve actions in the aftermath of the financial crisis were largely symbolic in consequence
questions.context: Austrians see the post-2008 response as the opposite of the medicine ABCT calls for. The malinvestments weren't allowed to liquidate; banks were bailed out; rates went to zero. The next cycle was baked in. The 2021-2023 inflation was the downstream consequence.

questions.question: Greenspan's October 23, 2008 testimony before Henry Waxman's committee said he had been in 'shocked disbelief' that his model had a flaw. What did Greenspan confess he had wrongly believed?
questions.answer: Lending institutions' self-interest would protect shareholders — additional regulation or oversight wasn't required
choices: Lending institutions' self-interest would protect shareholders — additional regulation or oversight wasn't required
ABCT was wrong — Greenspan testified that the Austrian framework had finally been vindicated by the 2008 events
His Ayn Rand career had blinded him — Greenspan repudiated his entire economic philosophy that day in detail
Lehman should have been saved — Greenspan said he regretted advising against a Lehman bailout the prior month
questions.context: Greenspan's testimony said his model had a flaw — about market self-regulation, not monetary policy. The confession left the deeper question of whether HE had caused the bubble (by holding rates at 1% in 2003-04) untouched.

questions.question: Frédéric Bastiat's 1850 pamphlet 'That Which Is Seen and That Which Is Not Seen' opens with a broken-window scenario. A shopkeeper's window is smashed; a crowd consoles him by saying it 'creates work for the glazier.' What's Bastiat's deeper point?
questions.answer: The window-fix money would have bought shoes or books — glazier work is visible but other tradesmen suffer hidden loss
choices: The window-fix money would have bought shoes or books — glazier work is visible but other tradesmen suffer hidden loss
The window-fix creates double employment — both glazier and shoemaker benefit from the broken-window scenario together
The window-fix proves economic growth — destruction always raises GDP figures in the year that immediately follows
The window-fix has no real effect — Bastiat believed all economic activity nets to zero across actors and time
questions.context: Bastiat 1850 is the founding statement of opportunity-cost reasoning in popular form. Henry Hazlitt's 'Economics in One Lesson' (1946) is the modern restatement. The 'broken window fallacy' name comes from Bastiat directly.

questions.question: Bastiat's 1850 'The Law' attacks what he calls 'legal plunder' — the use of law to transfer property from one citizen to another for the benefit of the second. He gives a test for spotting it. What's the test?
questions.answer: Whether the law takes from one to give to another — what the first didn't owe and what the second didn't earn
choices: Whether the law takes from one to give to another — what the first didn't owe and what the second didn't earn
Whether the law was passed unanimously — legal plunder only exists where a single legislator voted against the measure
Whether the law applies equally — Bastiat believed any uniform law was just regardless of its content or its effects
Whether the law was signed by a king — Bastiat thought all royal decrees were plunder and all legislative ones were just
questions.context: Bastiat's 'The Law' (June 1850, a few months before his death) is one of the most-translated classical-liberal pamphlets. The 'legal plunder' concept anticipates modern public-choice work on rent-seeking. Cato circulated millions of copies in the late 20th century.

questions.question: Bastiat's 1845 'Candle Makers' Petition' satirized French candle and lamp makers petitioning Parliament against 'unfair competition from a foreign rival supplying light at a price absurdly below our own.' Who is this rival?
questions.answer: The Sun — Bastiat shows that protection-from-competition arguments, if consistent, demand a law shuttering sunlight
choices: The Sun — Bastiat shows that protection-from-competition arguments, if consistent, demand a law shuttering sunlight
The British — Bastiat's pamphlet directly named English candle exporters as the threat to French manufacturers in 1845
The Belgians — Bastiat argued that small French-speaking neighbors were undercutting Paris candle makers via dumping
The Russians — Bastiat believed Tsarist suppliers were the main competitive threat to French candle manufacturing then
questions.context: The 'Candlemakers' Petition' is the most famous reductio ad absurdum in economic literature. By treating the Sun as the unfair foreign competitor, Bastiat exposes the absurdity of protectionist arguments. Read at every intro free-trade lecture for 175 years.

questions.question: A construction crew tears down an old building. A bystander says 'good, that creates work.' Bastiat's method tells you how to think about this claim. Where does the seen-vs-unseen analysis lead?
questions.answer: The torn building was past saved labor and capital — destroying it consumes what existed; it doesn't create wealth
choices: The torn building was past saved labor and capital — destroying it consumes what existed; it doesn't create wealth
The new project is bigger — so destruction always pays for itself when modernization is the goal of the redevelopment
Construction jobs pay better than demolition jobs — so the net effect is positive for the local labor market overall
Tax revenues from new construction exceed lost property taxes — so government always profits from urban demolition
questions.context: Bastiat's method generalizes to every 'destruction is good for the economy' claim — wars, natural disasters, planned obsolescence. The visible activity is real; the invisible loss (what the resources WOULD have built had they not been spent fixing destruction) is larger.

questions.question: Bastiat's 1850 essay sourced the famous line: 'The bad economist confines himself to the visible effect; the good economist takes into account both the effect that can be seen and those that must be foreseen.' What broader habit does this prescribe?
questions.answer: Track second-order effects — what the visible action prevents from happening, not just what it makes happen
choices: Track second-order effects — what the visible action prevents from happening, not just what it makes happen
Trust government statistics — Bastiat thought official numbers were the only reliable measure of true economic activity
Avoid theoretical reasoning — Bastiat said economists should rely only on direct observation of factories and markets
Use mathematical proofs — Bastiat believed every economic claim should be supported by formal algebraic derivation
questions.context: Henry Hazlitt's 'Economics in One Lesson' (1946) opens by quoting this passage and explicitly extending Bastiat. Thomas Sowell often calls 'thinking past the first stage' the defining habit of an economist. All three are running the same playbook.

questions.question: A town passes a 'buy local' ordinance: city money must be spent at city businesses, not on cheaper goods from elsewhere. Supporters say it 'keeps wealth in the community.' Apply Bastiat's seen-and-unseen method. What does it reveal?
questions.answer: Higher prices reduce what residents can buy elsewhere — the loss to those other tradesmen is hidden, but real
choices: Higher prices reduce what residents can buy elsewhere — the loss to those other tradesmen is hidden, but real
The town becomes wealthier — by recycling its own money internally with no compensating loss to outside trade
Local jobs grow without bound — Bastiat's method confirms that buy-local laws produce net employment gains
Outside merchants benefit too — protectionism between towns always produces win-win outcomes through specialization
questions.context: The 'buy local' argument is a small-scale version of the protectionist fallacy Bastiat dissected. Money 'kept in the community' at a higher price is money the community can't spend on other things. The seen benefit (local sales) hides the unseen cost.

questions.question: Richard Cantillon was an Irish-French banker who made a fortune trading John Law's Mississippi Bubble shares before the 1720 crash. His posthumous 'Essai' (1755) made a key observation. What is the 'Cantillon effect'?
questions.answer: New money enters at specific points — early recipients buy at OLD prices; by the time it ripples out, prices have risen
choices: New money enters at specific points — early recipients buy at OLD prices; by the time it ripples out, prices have risen
New money raises all prices simultaneously — Cantillon's law states monetary expansion is exactly neutral across actors
New money is destroyed by trade — Cantillon argued that international commerce eliminates monetary expansion's effects
New money causes deflation — Cantillon's paradox holds that printing more currency always reduces the price level
questions.context: Cantillon (~1680-1734) predates Adam Smith by half a century. He survived the Law bubble that ruined many of his clients. The Essai was published 21 years after his death and influenced French and Scottish classical economics deeply.

questions.question: John Law's 1719-1720 Mississippi Company scheme issued paper notes against speculative future French Louisiana profits. Cantillon, who knew Law personally, observed something his contemporaries missed about who benefited.
questions.answer: Those closest to the new money — bankers, court favorites, insiders profited; ordinary holders lost as prices rose later
choices: Those closest to the new money — bankers, court favorites, insiders profited; ordinary holders lost as prices rose later
Everyone benefited equally — the Mississippi notes circulated so smoothly that distribution effects didn't exist in practice
Only foreign holders benefited — Cantillon believed only Dutch and English investors profited from the Mississippi scheme
Only the French king benefited — all gains went to the crown rather than to any private participants involved
questions.context: Cantillon walked out of Law's bubble with a fortune, in part because he saw who got the new money first. The pattern — early recipients win, late recipients lose — is what modern Austrians call the Cantillon effect. The redistributive shadow of every monetary expansion.

questions.question: Apply the Cantillon effect to the 2020 US response to COVID. The Fed expanded its balance sheet by trillions; federal deficits ran multi-trillions; asset prices rose sharply through 2021. What does the Cantillon view say happened?
questions.answer: Asset holders and large financial firms benefited first — wage earners and savers saw the cost arrive later as inflation
choices: Asset holders and large financial firms benefited first — wage earners and savers saw the cost arrive later as inflation
All Americans benefited equally — pandemic stimulus checks distributed new money evenly across income brackets nationwide
Only the poorest benefited — the EITC and child credit changes meant low-income households gained disproportionately well
Nobody benefited — pandemic monetary expansion was sterile and produced no distributional effects of any sort whatsoever
questions.context: The 2020-2022 cycle was Cantillon-textbook. Asset prices rose first (Wall Street, real estate, crypto). CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, hitting savers and wage earners hardest. The redistribution from late to early recipients was massive.

questions.question: The Cantillon effect explains a paradox: monetary inflation is often called a 'tax on the poor,' yet official inflation measures sometimes look modest while asset prices roar. Why does the Cantillon framework predict this?
questions.answer: Early recipients bid up assets first — CPI tracks consumer goods, missing the asset-price effect that hits savers hardest
choices: Early recipients bid up assets first — CPI tracks consumer goods, missing the asset-price effect that hits savers hardest
Inflation only counts grocery prices — official CPI excludes all financial products by design across every published measure
The poor own no assets — therefore monetary expansion cannot affect them in any direct or indirect way whatsoever
CPI is fabricated — there is no actual measurement of consumer prices in any developed economy in any year at all
questions.context: This Cantillon framing is why Austrians argue inflation is regressive even when CPI looks tame. House prices, stock indices, and crypto soaking up new money is a wealth transfer from those who don't own these assets to those who do. The tax is real.

questions.question: Cantillon's 1755 'Essai' was rediscovered by William Stanley Jevons in 1881 and called 'the cradle of political economy.' It predated Smith's 'Wealth of Nations' by decades. Why has his name remained obscure?
questions.answer: Published posthumously, in French, narrowly circulated — Smith's 1776 work in English to a popular audience eclipsed it
choices: Published posthumously, in French, narrowly circulated — Smith's 1776 work in English to a popular audience eclipsed it
His work was discredited — modern econometric testing showed his observations were statistically false across every study
He was a fraud — modern scholarship has demonstrated that Cantillon did not write the Essai attributed to his name
His work covered only banking — Cantillon never discussed broader markets or division of labor in any of his writings
questions.context: Cantillon was murdered in London in 1734 (probably by a disgruntled chef, though the case is unsolved). His manuscript circulated in French intellectual circles before publication. Smith's 1776 work, in English to a popular Scottish audience, eclipsed it in fame.

questions.question: Murray Rothbard arrived at New York University in 1956 as a freshly-minted PhD with Joseph Dorfman on his committee. His dissertation was published in 1963 as a deeply Austrian reinterpretation of one specific US event. What event?
questions.answer: The Great Depression — 'America's Great Depression' argued the Fed caused the 1929 crash through 1920s credit expansion
choices: The Great Depression — 'America's Great Depression' argued the Fed caused the 1929 crash through 1920s credit expansion
The Civil War — Rothbard's dissertation analyzed Lincoln's economic policies and Northern industrial finance through 1865
The Spanish-American War — Rothbard examined McKinley's gold-standard politics and Cuban sugar trade arrangements then
The Whiskey Rebellion — Rothbard reinterpreted Washington-era frontier economics and federal taxation under Hamilton
questions.context: Rothbard's 'America's Great Depression' (1963) applies ABCT to the 1929 crash and 1930s slump. He blames Fed credit expansion in the 1920s, Hoover's interventions (not Roosevelt's, mostly), and the slow liquidation pattern. Foundational for modern Austrian macro.

questions.question: Thomas Sowell entered Chicago for his PhD in the late 1960s. His dissertation supervisor was Milton Friedman, and he completed his degree in 1968. What broader intellectual journey had Sowell taken before arriving at Chicago?
questions.answer: From Marxism — Sowell had been a Marxist as a young man and reasoned his way out through evidence and study
choices: From Marxism — Sowell had been a Marxist as a young man and reasoned his way out through evidence and study
From Keynesianism — Sowell had been a leading New Deal advocate before switching to monetarism at Chicago
From Austrian school — Sowell had been a Misesian and converted to Chicago monetarism under Friedman's influence
From mainstream — Sowell had no prior school commitment and chose Chicago for its location rather than philosophy
questions.context: Sowell describes his journey in 'A Personal Odyssey' (2000). The Department of Labor internship (1961) — observing how minimum-wage policy actually played out — was the decisive moment. The data didn't fit the Marxist theory. Sowell followed the evidence.

questions.question: Thomas Sowell's 'Knowledge and Decisions' (1980) is widely considered his magnum opus. Sowell himself called it 'the most important book I have written.' What's its central argument, built on Hayek 1945?
questions.answer: Different decision systems handle dispersed knowledge differently — markets process it better than committees do
choices: Different decision systems handle dispersed knowledge differently — markets process it better than committees do
Knowledge is impossible — Sowell's 1980 book argues no decision-maker ever has enough information to choose anything
Education solves all problems — Sowell argued more universal schooling would eliminate every economic and social ill
Government must coordinate — Sowell's book proposes a national database to pool knowledge across decision-makers fully
questions.context: Sowell explicitly built 'Knowledge and Decisions' on Hayek 1945. The book extends the price-system insight to ALL decision-making institutions: families, firms, governments, courts. The trade-offs in how knowledge gets processed determine which institutions perform well.

questions.question: Murray Rothbard ran a weekly Monday-night seminar in his Manhattan apartment from the 1960s through his death in 1995. Hoppe, Block, Salerno passed through. What broader role did the seminar serve?
questions.answer: Kept the Austrian school alive — Mises died 1973, programs ignored Austrian work, Rothbard sustained the network
choices: Kept the Austrian school alive — Mises died 1973, programs ignored Austrian work, Rothbard sustained the network
Was purely social — Rothbard's Monday-night gatherings were not actually about economics in any substantive way
Was Marxist — Rothbard ran a Trotskyist study circle until his death, in opposition to his published economic work
Was tiny — Rothbard's seminar had only one or two attendees and produced no lasting intellectual influence at all
questions.context: Rothbard's Monday-night seminars produced the next generation of Austrian scholars. Combined with the Mises Institute (founded 1982 at Auburn) and the Foundation for Economic Education, this private infrastructure carried the school through Keynesian-monetarist dominance.

questions.question: Thomas Sowell's 1981 'Ethnic America' surveyed immigrant groups — Jewish, Italian, Irish, Chinese, German, Black. Sowell drew a conclusion that ran against the dominant 1981 explanation of group differences. What was the finding?
questions.answer: Cultural patterns from each group's origin — explained outcomes more than discrimination alone could account for
choices: Cultural patterns from each group's origin — explained outcomes more than discrimination alone could account for
Discrimination explained everything — Sowell concluded that the only causal factor in group outcomes was racial bias
Genetics explained the differences — Sowell's 1981 book argued for heritable IQ as the master variable across groups
Geography explained the differences — Sowell argued that climate alone determined the economic success of every group
questions.context: Sowell's empirical comparative work spans 'Ethnic America' (1981), 'Migrations and Cultures' (1996), 'Conquests and Cultures' (1998). The pattern across his books: cultural endowments transferred from origins predict outcomes more than current discrimination does.

questions.question: Rothbard helped found the Libertarian Party in 1971 but broke with it in 1989 over what he called 'modal libertarianism.' What was his complaint?
questions.answer: Drift from a working-class populist base — toward an upscale cosmopolitan posture he considered politically dead
choices: Drift from a working-class populist base — toward an upscale cosmopolitan posture he considered politically dead
The party had become too friendly to Marxism — Rothbard thought it had embraced Soviet-style central planning by 1980
The party had abandoned Austrian economics — Rothbard objected that LP platforms endorsed Keynesian deficit spending
The party had endorsed Reagan — Rothbard objected to the LP supporting any Republican presidential candidate in any year
questions.context: Rothbard's 1989 break led to the 'paleolibertarian' move with Lew Rockwell — an attempt to root libertarianism in conservative working-class culture rather than upper-middle-class lifestyle politics. The John Randolph Club emerged from this realignment.

questions.question: Sowell's 'A Conflict of Visions' (1987) distinguishes two ways of seeing human nature and society. Sowell argues most political disagreements come from this divide. What are his two visions?
questions.answer: Constrained — human nature is fixed, trade-offs inevitable — versus unconstrained — nature is improvable, solutions exist
choices: Constrained — human nature is fixed, trade-offs inevitable — versus unconstrained — nature is improvable, solutions exist
Capitalist — markets work freely — versus socialist — government must own all means of production at every scale
Religious — God designs society — versus secular — humans alone construct the social order without divine input
American — open society — versus European — closed society — Sowell's central distinction is geographic in nature
questions.context: Sowell's 'A Conflict of Visions' (1987, revised 2007) identifies Burke, Hayek, Hamilton, and Friedman as constrained-vision thinkers; Rousseau, Godwin, Veblen as unconstrained. Widely assigned in political philosophy and explains the moral structure of left-right disagreement.

questions.question: Murray Rothbard's 'Man, Economy, and State' (1962) was conceived as a textbook expansion of Mises's 'Human Action' (1949). Rothbard takes one further step Mises didn't fully take. What additional move does Rothbard make?
questions.answer: Extends praxeology consistently to government — treating the state as just another actor pursuing its own interests
choices: Extends praxeology consistently to government — treating the state as just another actor pursuing its own interests
Rejects Mises's methodology — Rothbard's 1962 textbook replaces praxeology with empirical statistical methods entirely
Endorses Keynesianism — Rothbard incorporates aggregate-demand reasoning into the Austrian framework throughout his work
Embraces Marxism — Rothbard's textbook accepts the labor theory of value alongside Austrian subjective marginalism
questions.context: Rothbard's extension into anarcho-capitalism comes from applying Mises's praxeology consistently. If individual action is the foundation, government can't be exempt from the same analysis. This is one of Rothbard's most controversial moves within the Austrian school.

questions.question: James Buchanan and Gordon Tullock published 'The Calculus of Consent' in 1962. The book applies economic methodology — rational self-interest, marginal analysis — to politics. Why was this disruptive?
questions.answer: Mainstream theories treated officials as benevolent guardians — Buchanan-Tullock said they have their own interests like anyone
choices: Mainstream theories treated officials as benevolent guardians — Buchanan-Tullock said they have their own interests like anyone
Mainstream theories treated politics as random — Buchanan-Tullock said voting outcomes were determined by lunar cycles alone
Mainstream theories ignored markets — Buchanan-Tullock said only markets matter and politics is irrelevant to outcomes
Mainstream theories used math — Buchanan-Tullock rejected all formal analysis in favor of purely narrative descriptions
questions.context: Public choice theory dissolved the 'market failure → benevolent government fix' framing dominating postwar welfare economics. Treating the political agent as self-interested, you must compare imperfect markets to imperfect governments, not idealized planners.

questions.question: Gordon Tullock's 1967 paper 'The Welfare Costs of Tariffs, Monopolies, and Theft' coined what's now called 'rent-seeking,' formalized by Anne Krueger in 1974. What does rent-seeking refer to?
questions.answer: Spending real resources to capture political privileges — like lobbying for a tariff that benefits one firm at others' expense
choices: Spending real resources to capture political privileges — like lobbying for a tariff that benefits one firm at others' expense
Renting office space in Washington DC — Tullock's narrow term for the geographic concentration of lobbying activity
Charging high prices for goods — rent-seeking meant firms that priced above marginal cost in Tullock's original usage
Collecting rents from tenants — Tullock used the term in his 1967 paper to describe ordinary landlord-tenant relationships
questions.context: The 'rent' in rent-seeking is economic rent — payments above what's needed to bring a resource to market. Lobbying for a sugar quota costs real lawyer-hours and PR — that's deadweight loss, on top of the price distortion. Tullock's insight is that this triangle is big.

questions.question: Buchanan won the 1986 Nobel for public choice work. His Nobel lecture criticized something specific about postwar economics. What was the critique?
questions.answer: Postwar economics modeled markets carefully — but treated government as a perfect optimizer; that asymmetry was incoherent
choices: Postwar economics modeled markets carefully — but treated government as a perfect optimizer; that asymmetry was incoherent
Postwar economics relied too heavily on free markets — Buchanan argued for greatly increased federal regulatory authority
Postwar economics ignored psychology — Buchanan said behavioral models should replace rational choice in all applications
Postwar economics underweighted China — Buchanan claimed Western academics had ignored East Asian growth patterns entirely
questions.context: Buchanan's Nobel was awarded for 'his development of the contractual and constitutional bases for the theory of economic and political decision-making.' The 'symmetry' principle — same actor model in markets and politics — is the unifying methodological move of public choice.

questions.question: George Stigler's 'The Theory of Economic Regulation' (1971) extended public choice to a specific institutional pathology. Stigler argued regulatory agencies end up serving someone other than the public. Who?
questions.answer: The industries they regulate — incumbents capture regulators who become their gatekeepers against new entry
choices: The industries they regulate — incumbents capture regulators who become their gatekeepers against new entry
The general public — Stigler argued postwar regulatory agencies had remarkable success in serving consumer interests
The President — Stigler's 1971 paper argued that regulators always defer to executive branch policy preferences alone
Foreign governments — Stigler claimed Soviet and Chinese influence dominated US regulatory agencies after World War II
questions.context: Stigler's 'regulatory capture' became a foundational public-choice concept. The pattern — railroad regulators captured by railroads, broadcast regulators by broadcasters, banking regulators by banks — is observable across most major regulatory agencies. Stigler won the 1982 Nobel.

questions.question: Public choice predicts a structural problem with democratic decisions on policies with CONCENTRATED benefits but DIFFUSE costs — like a sugar quota. Why does democracy systematically produce these outcomes against the broader public?
questions.answer: Sugar producers gain a lot each, lobby intensely — consumers each lose a little, so most don't even notice the policy
choices: Sugar producers gain a lot each, lobby intensely — consumers each lose a little, so most don't even notice the policy
Sugar producers are more numerous than consumers — in any electorate, suppliers outvote buyers and so policy follows
Sugar producers are more articulate — they explain their interests in ways the typical consumer cannot comprehend at all
Sugar producers are wealthier — they bribe lawmakers directly, while consumers lack the resources to participate at all
questions.context: Organized minorities beat unorganized majorities on policies where the math of attention favors the concentrated side. US sugar quotas, ethanol mandates, dairy compacts — all examples. The diffuse loser doesn't fight because his individual stake is tiny.

questions.question: Ronald Coase's 1937 paper 'The Nature of the Firm' asked a question economists hadn't formally asked: if markets coordinate so well through prices, why do firms exist? Why don't we contract everything in markets?
questions.answer: Market transactions have costs — searching, negotiating, enforcing contracts — firms exist when those exceed in-house costs
choices: Market transactions have costs — searching, negotiating, enforcing contracts — firms exist when those exceed in-house costs
Firms exist because of regulation — without government-issued corporate charters, all production would happen through markets
Firms exist because of taxation — pre-1937 tax codes incentivized internal hierarchy over market-based coordination widely
Firms exist because of psychology — workers prefer being told what to do rather than negotiating each task individually
questions.context: Coase's 1937 paper introduced 'transaction costs' as a concept. He used the idea again in 'The Problem of Social Cost' (1960) to analyze externalities. Both papers were cited in his 1991 Nobel. Coase died in 2013 at age 102, still publishing.

questions.question: Coase's 1960 'The Problem of Social Cost' challenged the standard Pigouvian solution to externalities (taxes on the polluter). The 'Coase theorem' that emerged says something striking. What?
questions.answer: If transaction costs are low and rights are clear — parties negotiate to an efficient outcome regardless of who is initially liable
choices: If transaction costs are low and rights are clear — parties negotiate to an efficient outcome regardless of who is initially liable
Government always needs to set the pollution price — markets cannot ever reach efficient externality solutions on their own
Pollution is unsolvable — Coase's theorem argues that no possible institutional arrangement can address negative externalities
Property rights must be communally held — Coase argued individual ownership prevents efficient outcomes in any negotiation
questions.context: The Coase theorem reframed externality policy debates. Even when full Coase-bargain conditions don't hold (most of the time), the framing shifts attention from 'tax the polluter' to 'how should we assign and structure property rights so the bargain becomes feasible?'

questions.question: Milton Friedman's 1962 'Capitalism and Freedom' argues that economic freedom is necessary — though not always sufficient — for political freedom. What's the mechanism Friedman identifies?
questions.answer: Economic power dispersed in markets prevents concentration of all power in the state — a key check on political authority
choices: Economic power dispersed in markets prevents concentration of all power in the state — a key check on political authority
Economic prosperity makes voters happier — Friedman believed material wealth alone produces political-freedom outcomes
Economic exchange teaches reasoning — Friedman thought daily market participation made citizens more politically savvy
Economic specialization requires education — Friedman argued literacy spread through markets produced free political systems
questions.context: Friedman's central thesis: no society has been politically free without also being economically free, even though many economically-free societies have unfree politics. The relationship is one-way necessary. The book emerged from his Chicago lectures and became hugely influential.

questions.question: Friedman's 1968 American Economic Association presidential address introduced the 'natural rate of unemployment.' The concept refuted a then-mainstream policy claim. What claim did Friedman attack?
questions.answer: Central banks could permanently lower unemployment by tolerating slight inflation — the simple Phillips curve trade-off
choices: Central banks could permanently lower unemployment by tolerating slight inflation — the simple Phillips curve trade-off
That unemployment was caused by labor unions — Friedman argued union pressure was the only relevant variable
That unemployment was caused by automation — Friedman argued technology drove all postwar US joblessness data
That unemployment was a myth — Friedman's 1968 speech denied any meaningful concept of involuntary worker idleness
questions.context: Friedman's 1968 address (and Edmund Phelps's independent same-year work) predicted any inflation-unemployment trade-off would unravel as workers adjusted expectations. The 1970s stagflation — high inflation AND high unemployment — vindicated him; the simple Phillips curve was dead.

questions.question: Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz's 'A Monetary History of the United States 1867-1960' (1963) reinterpreted the Great Depression. Their argument: the Fed caused it. By how much did the US money supply contract from 1929 to 1933?
questions.answer: About one-third — the largest monetary contraction in US history, alongside ~9000 bank failures across those four years
choices: About one-third — the largest monetary contraction in US history, alongside ~9000 bank failures across those four years
About one percent — a normal seasonal variation that should not have produced any economic disturbance whatsoever
About a tenth of one percent — the money supply held steady through the Depression, refuting Friedman entirely outright
About one half of one percent — less than the supply had grown in the single year before the 1929 stock-market crash
questions.context: Friedman + Schwartz turned the Great Depression narrative inside out. The institution founded in 1913 to prevent banking panics presided over the worst banking collapse and economic catastrophe in US history. Friedman noted the Depression vindicates Mises 1912 and Hayek 1931.

questions.question: Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk's 'Capital and Interest' (1884) developed the Austrian theory of interest. Core idea: interest rates aren't arbitrary numbers set by banks. What do interest rates actually reflect?
questions.answer: Time preference — how much people value goods now versus the same goods later, varying across savers and borrowers
choices: Time preference — how much people value goods now versus the same goods later, varying across savers and borrowers
Inflation expectations — interest rates in Böhm-Bawerk's theory respond only to expected changes in the money supply
Political pressure — Böhm-Bawerk argued interest rates were set arbitrarily by governments and have no market basis
Risk premiums — the entirety of any interest rate reflects expected default probabilities and nothing else at all
questions.context: Böhm-Bawerk taught Mises, who taught Hayek and Rothbard. The time-preference theory is the foundation Austrians use to argue that central banks can't permanently lower rates — they can only mask the real time-preference reality, producing the distortions ABCT traces.

questions.question: Hayek used the concept of 'spontaneous order' to describe how complex systems emerge from many individual choices without any central designer. He argued this happens not just in markets but in three other domains. Which?
questions.answer: Language, common law, and customs — systems with rules nobody designed but everyone follows
choices: Language, common law, and customs — systems with rules nobody designed but everyone follows
Religion, military, and royalty — Hayek argued top-down designed institutions exhibit the same spontaneous-order properties
Astronomy, chemistry, and biology — Hayek thought the natural sciences were examples of spontaneous social order ultimately
Education, healthcare, and welfare — Hayek argued government-designed systems exemplify spontaneous-order principles broadly
questions.context: Hayek developed spontaneous order in 'Law, Legislation and Liberty' (1973-1979). The insight: complex coordination can happen without a coordinator. English common law evolved case by case. Languages drift across millions of speakers. None of this is designed; all of it is ordered.

questions.question: Carl Menger's 1871 'Principles of Economics' co-founded the marginal revolution alongside Jevons (England) and Walras (Lausanne). Menger's specific contribution was a value theory that overturned the classical labor theory. What's the Mengerian view?
questions.answer: Value is subjective — set by each individual's ranking of how a good serves their particular ends at the margin
choices: Value is subjective — set by each individual's ranking of how a good serves their particular ends at the margin
Value is objective — set by the total labor hours needed to produce a good, summed across all stages of production
Value is conventional — set by tradition and legal custom rather than by either labor or marginal individual judgment
Value is impossible to determine — Menger's 1871 book denied any meaningful theory of value could be developed
questions.context: Menger's subjective value theory dissolves the 'diamonds vs water' paradox classical economists had struggled with. Water is more useful in total, but the FIRST diamond serves a higher-ranked end for most people than the THOUSANDTH glass of water. Marginal subjective value.

questions.question: Mises's 1922 'Socialism' is a 500-page expansion of his 1920 calculation argument. The book addressed not just economic but moral and cultural critiques of socialism. It famously converted one prominent thinker. Who?
questions.answer: Friedrich Hayek — Hayek said reading Mises's 'Socialism' in his Vienna student years changed his political-economic views
choices: Friedrich Hayek — Hayek said reading Mises's 'Socialism' in his Vienna student years changed his political-economic views
John Maynard Keynes — Keynes read Mises in 1922 and converted from Fabian socialism to free-market economics in that year
Joseph Stalin — Stalin reportedly read Mises's 'Socialism' in 1923 and quietly modified Soviet economic policy in response
Karl Marx — Marx encountered Mises's 1922 book and retracted his earlier 'Capital' in a posthumous addendum that year
questions.context: Hayek wrote in tribute that reading Mises's 'Socialism' was decisive for his intellectual development. The book ran in multiple editions, was translated widely, and made Mises an internationally controversial figure. Marx had died in 1883; Keynes never converted.

questions.question: Mises ran a 'Privatseminar' in Vienna 1920-1934 — a weekly evening seminar at his Chamber of Commerce office. Who passed through this remarkable gathering?
questions.answer: Hayek, Machlup, Morgenstern, Haberler, Voegelin, Schütz, Kaufmann — many future giants of economics and social theory
choices: Hayek, Machlup, Morgenstern, Haberler, Voegelin, Schütz, Kaufmann — many future giants of economics and social theory
Lenin, Trotsky, and Stalin — the Mises Kreis was secretly the meeting place for the early Bolshevik leadership in Europe
Freud, Jung, and Adler — Mises's seminar was actually a psychoanalysis circle disguised as economic discussion sessions
Wittgenstein, Heidegger, Carnap — the Mises Kreis attracted exclusively philosophers without any economists involved
questions.context: The Mises Kreis (1920-1934) was a giant of interwar Vienna's intellectual life. When Mises emigrated under Nazi threat in 1934, the circle dispersed across Europe and America. Several members became Nobel laureates or founders of distinct schools in their own fields.

questions.question: Hayek's 'The Road to Serfdom' (1944) was a wartime book to the British public. It argued economic central planning leads by its own internal logic to political authoritarianism. What's the mechanism Hayek identified?
questions.answer: Planners must agree on goals — with no spontaneous consensus, plans require coercion; the worst-tempered rise to the top
choices: Planners must agree on goals — with no spontaneous consensus, plans require coercion; the worst-tempered rise to the top
Planning fails economically — voters then reject the planning party and elect authoritarian leaders to restore prosperity
Planning is too efficient — once people see how well the plan works, they vote to give the planners more political power
Planning is unrelated to politics — Hayek's 1944 book has been broadly misinterpreted by readers across the spectrum
questions.context: Hayek's argument: comprehensive economic plans require consensus on ends; democratic consensus doesn't form for detailed plans; planners must therefore choose; choosing requires coercion; coercion attracts certain personalities. The chapter 'Why the Worst Get on Top' is the crystallization.

questions.question: Henry Hazlitt's 1946 book 'Economics in One Lesson' restated Bastiat for a postwar American audience. The book's 'one lesson' is captured in a single sentence. What is it?
questions.answer: The art of economics consists in looking at the longer effects of any act or policy, and at all groups, not just one
choices: The art of economics consists in looking at the longer effects of any act or policy, and at all groups, not just one
Economics shows that government spending always pays for itself if directed to socially useful purposes by experts
Economics demonstrates that all market prices are wrong, since only experts can determine the true value of goods
Economics proves that free trade is impossible, since every country needs tariffs to maintain employment levels at home
questions.context: Hazlitt's book is the most widely-read popular-economics text of the 20th century — millions of copies, dozens of translations. The lesson distills Bastiat's seen-and-unseen method into a single discipline: extend reasoning to all groups and all time horizons before judging a policy.

questions.question: The Bitcoin Genesis block was mined on January 3, 2009, with a coinbase reward of 50 BTC. These 50 coins are provably unspendable — no private key can ever spend them. Why does this matter for Bitcoin's design?
questions.answer: Proves no founder can spend the first coins — the 'immaculate conception' criticism is defused at block zero
choices: Proves no founder can spend the first coins — the 'immaculate conception' criticism is defused at block zero
Was a bug — Satoshi tried to spend the coins later but couldn't because of a programming error in the original code
Was for tax reasons — Satoshi chose unspendable coins to avoid capital gains liability in his home country at launch
Was a security measure — Satoshi wanted to test whether the network could function without the first reward being moved
questions.context: The Genesis-block 50 BTC sits at address 1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa, forever unspendable. This is a deliberate engineering choice and a credibility move — no pre-mine, no founder allocation, no hidden treasury. The supply curve starts at block one with no exception.

questions.question: The Bitcoin Genesis block's coinbase transaction contained an embedded message: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks.' The headline is from that day's London Times. Why did Satoshi embed it?
questions.answer: Dual purpose — timestamps the chain to a date AND signals Bitcoin's response to bank bailouts taking place that week
choices: Dual purpose — timestamps the chain to a date AND signals Bitcoin's response to bank bailouts taking place that week
Satoshi was paid by The Times for the placement — the embedded headline was a paid promotional placement that week
Bitcoin's protocol requires every block to cite a newspaper — with the Genesis simply being the first in this series
The message was decryption-only — the actual purpose was to test whether nodes could read embedded ASCII text strings
questions.context: The Times headline serves a dual purpose: it cryptographically proves the chain couldn't have been mined before January 3, 2009, and it editorializes the reason Bitcoin exists. The bailout context is part of Bitcoin's founding statement, encoded in block zero forever.

questions.question: Block 170 of the Bitcoin blockchain, mined January 12, 2009, recorded the first Bitcoin transaction: Satoshi sent 10 BTC to someone else. Who was the recipient — the first person to receive Bitcoin?
questions.answer: Hal Finney — cryptographer, RPOW developer, the first person besides Satoshi to run the Bitcoin software downloaded
choices: Hal Finney — cryptographer, RPOW developer, the first person besides Satoshi to run the Bitcoin software downloaded
Wei Dai — author of b-money 1998, to whom Satoshi sent the first transaction as scientific credit for prior work
Adam Back — Hashcash creator 1997, who became the second Bitcoin node operator after exchanging emails with Satoshi
Nick Szabo — bit gold designer 2005, often suspected of being Satoshi but receiving the first transaction officially
questions.context: Hal Finney (1956-2014) was a cryptographic pioneer at the PGP Corporation. He downloaded the Bitcoin software on January 11, 2009, and received Satoshi's first transfer the next day. Finney died of ALS in 2014; he was cryonically preserved by Alcor.

questions.question: On May 22, 2010, programmer Laszlo Hanyecz posted on Bitcointalk offering 10,000 BTC for two pizzas. Jeremy Sturdivant accepted; two Papa John's pizzas were delivered to Hanyecz's home in Jacksonville. What date is now celebrated?
questions.answer: Bitcoin Pizza Day — May 22 each year commemorates the first commercial Bitcoin transaction for a real-world good
choices: Bitcoin Pizza Day — May 22 each year commemorates the first commercial Bitcoin transaction for a real-world good
Bitcoin Genesis Day — May 22 marks the anniversary of the first block being mined the previous year in 2009
Bitcoin Halving Day — May 22 is the anniversary of the first halving event in the Bitcoin protocol's history
Bitcoin Tax Day — May 22 became known as the day the IRS first ruled Bitcoin transactions to be taxable events
questions.context: The 10,000 BTC pizzas would be worth around half a billion dollars at Bitcoin's late-2024 prices. Hanyecz has said he doesn't regret it — somebody had to demonstrate Bitcoin could pay for real things. Pizza Day has become a major community holiday.

questions.question: The Bitcoin white paper was posted to a cryptography mailing list on October 31, 2008. 9 pages long, titled 'Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System.' What specific problem does the paper claim to solve?
questions.answer: The double-spending problem — preventing digital money from being copied and spent twice without a trusted intermediary
choices: The double-spending problem — preventing digital money from being copied and spent twice without a trusted intermediary
The encryption problem — scrambling financial messages so that only the recipient can decode the transaction content
The speed problem — settling payments faster than banks could process them during the financial crisis years
The privacy problem — making all transactions completely anonymous and untraceable across the global network
questions.context: Double-spend was the open challenge in digital cash before Bitcoin. DigiCash (Chaum 1989) needed a central issuer. B-money (Dai 1998) and bit gold (Szabo 2005) sketched solutions but couldn't fully implement them. The white paper's combination of proof-of-work + a public ledger solved it.

questions.question: Satoshi Nakamoto disappeared from Bitcoin in April 2011. The last verified message — sent to Mike Hearn — said only 'I've moved on to other things.' Satoshi's identity has never been confirmed. What's the recognition skill about this absence?
questions.answer: A protocol with no founder cannot be coerced by capturing one — leaderlessness is part of Bitcoin's credible neutrality
choices: A protocol with no founder cannot be coerced by capturing one — leaderlessness is part of Bitcoin's credible neutrality
Bitcoin without Satoshi is rudderless — the protocol cannot upgrade itself and is destined to fail without his return
Satoshi must be a government agency — only a state actor would deliberately hide its identity after launching a project
Bitcoin without Satoshi is illegal — the protocol cannot meet regulatory requirements without an identifiable founder
questions.context: Satoshi's voluntary departure left Bitcoin in a unique position: no founder to subpoena, sue, or pressure. The Satoshi-owned coins (estimated ~1 million BTC across early blocks) have never moved. The combination of unspendable Genesis + dormant founder coins anchors Bitcoin's credibility.

questions.question: Bitcoin's block subsidy halves every 210,000 blocks — about every four years. The schedule progressed: 50 → 25 → 12.5 → 6.25 → 3.125 BTC per block. When does issuance reach effectively zero?
questions.answer: Around 2140 — the last fractional satoshi is expected to be mined then, capping supply near 21 million BTC
choices: Around 2140 — the last fractional satoshi is expected to be mined then, capping supply near 21 million BTC
Around 2050 — the schedule was accelerated by the 2017 SegWit upgrade and the 2021 Taproot soft fork combined
Around 2200 — the halving period was extended to 50 years in a 2015 protocol update by Bitcoin Core developers
It never reaches zero — Bitcoin's protocol allows the block reward to continue indefinitely under a recent update
questions.context: The geometric series 50 + 25 + 12.5 + ... converges to 100, meaning total mined BTC approaches 50 × 210,000 × 2 = 21 million. The last block reward becomes a single satoshi (10^-8 BTC), then drops to zero. Around block 6,930,000 — projected around 2140.

questions.question: Bitcoin's halving dates so far: 2012 (50→25), 2016 (25→12.5), 2020 (12.5→6.25), 2024 (6.25→3.125). The 2024 halving happened in April. What's specifically guaranteed about the supply schedule, regardless of who mines or trades?
questions.answer: Set in code — no central party can change it; only network-wide consensus could ever alter the schedule
choices: Set in code — no central party can change it; only network-wide consensus could ever alter the schedule
Set by the Bitcoin Foundation — a board of directors votes on each halving's effective date and exact quantity
Set by the Federal Reserve — Bitcoin's issuance schedule was synchronized with Fed rate decisions after 2020
Set by major miners — pools controlling more than 51% of hashrate can vote to delay each halving in turn
questions.context: The Bitcoin issuance schedule is a feature of the protocol code that every full node enforces independently. Changing it would require a hard fork that the majority of nodes refuse to upgrade to — economically very unlikely. The supply curve is mathematically certain.

questions.question: Bitcoin's supply cap is approximately 21 million BTC. As of late 2024, around 19.7 million have been mined. The cap isn't exactly 21M because of rounding in the halving schedule. What's the precise figure?
questions.answer: Approximately 20,999,999.9769 BTC — the maximum approaches but never quite reaches 21M due to integer truncation
choices: Approximately 20,999,999.9769 BTC — the maximum approaches but never quite reaches 21M due to integer truncation
Exactly 21,000,000.0000 BTC — the supply hits exactly this value at the projected final block height in the future
Approximately 22,500,000 BTC — the cap was raised by a 2017 SegWit-era amendment to the Bitcoin protocol code
Approximately 18,500,000 BTC — the cap was lowered when several million coins were determined to be permanently lost
questions.context: Halving rewards get rounded down to satoshis (10^-8 BTC) at each step, so the geometric sum doesn't reach a clean 21M. The exact supply approaches ~20,999,999.97690000 BTC. The 21M figure is a shorthand. The hard cap is a feature of the protocol, not a design intention added later.

questions.question: Bitcoin's 21M supply cap is enforced by every full node. If a miner produced a block containing more than the allowed subsidy, what would happen?
questions.answer: Other nodes would reject the block as invalid — the miner would have wasted electricity producing an orphan block
choices: Other nodes would reject the block as invalid — the miner would have wasted electricity producing an orphan block
The block would be accepted with a warning — Bitcoin Core logs the violation but does not stop the propagation
The block would be accepted normally — supply-cap enforcement is the responsibility of exchanges, not of nodes
The block would be flagged for the Bitcoin Foundation — which then votes whether to ratify the bonus issuance
questions.context: Every full node independently validates the subsidy against the height-dependent rule. A block exceeding the allowed reward is invalid; honest nodes refuse to relay or build on it. The cap isn't a policy enforced from above — it's a property of the consensus rules every node checks.

questions.question: Bitcoin's halving is sometimes called the 'stock-to-flow' event. The stock-to-flow ratio compares existing supply (stock) to new annual production (flow). After each halving, what happens to Bitcoin's stock-to-flow ratio?
questions.answer: It approximately doubles — flow is cut in half while stock keeps growing, raising the ratio sharply each cycle
choices: It approximately doubles — flow is cut in half while stock keeps growing, raising the ratio sharply each cycle
It approximately halves — both stock and flow shrink in unison, leaving the ratio approximately stable over time
It remains constant — the Bitcoin protocol adjusts the stock variable to compensate for changes in the flow component
It approaches zero — every halving brings Bitcoin closer to a stock-to-flow value of zero by mathematical definition
questions.context: Plan B's stock-to-flow model (2019) attempted to predict Bitcoin price from this ratio. The model has been criticized empirically — but the underlying observation, that Bitcoin's stock-to-flow doubles every four years and approaches gold's ratio (and then exceeds it), is a real property of the schedule.

questions.question: Bitcoin's fixed 21M supply cap stands in sharp contrast to fiat, whose supply expands at central-bank discretion. Why does the cap make Bitcoin a fundamentally different kind of monetary asset, in Austrian terms?
questions.answer: Sound money requires inelastic supply — Bitcoin's cap makes it the first digitally-native programmatically-scarce asset
choices: Sound money requires inelastic supply — Bitcoin's cap makes it the first digitally-native programmatically-scarce asset
