Bitcoin is identical to fiat — the supply cap can be raised by the Bitcoin Foundation board through ordinary majority votes
Bitcoin is inferior to fiat — the inelastic supply prevents needed expansion during economic downturns and recessions
Bitcoin is only philosophically scarce — the actual cap is enforced by social custom and could be changed informally
questions.context: Saifedean Ammous's 'The Bitcoin Standard' (2018) is the canonical popular treatment of Bitcoin as Austrian sound money. The combination — programmatically scarce, no issuer, credibly neutral, fair-launched — has no historical precedent. Gold's supply still grows ~1.5% per year.

questions.question: After 2140 — when the last satoshi is mined — Bitcoin miners receive no block subsidy. The protocol nonetheless expects miners to continue securing the network. How will mining remain profitable?
questions.answer: Transaction fees alone — block-space demand replaces the subsidy as the network's security budget
choices: Transaction fees alone — block-space demand replaces the subsidy as the network's security budget
A new subsidy will be voted in — the Bitcoin Foundation will restart issuance through governance once the cap is reached
Mining will cease entirely — the network is expected to stop processing transactions after the year 2140 by design
Government grants will fund mining — central banks worldwide are preparing to subsidize Bitcoin security after 2140
questions.context: The fee-only future is the model Bitcoin is heading toward. As subsidy declines (halving by halving), the fee share of miner revenue grows. The economic question is whether block-space demand will be high enough to sustain security — an active research question.

questions.question: Bitcoin's 21M cap means terminal inflation is zero. During issuance, the inflation rate decreases at each halving. Roughly what was Bitcoin's annualized inflation rate immediately after the April 2024 halving?
questions.answer: Around 0.83% — lower than gold's ~1.5%, making Bitcoin's stock-to-flow exceed gold's for the first time ever
choices: Around 0.83% — lower than gold's ~1.5%, making Bitcoin's stock-to-flow exceed gold's for the first time ever
Around 5% — equivalent to the typical US dollar inflation rate during the 2021-2022 period of pandemic policy
Around 12% — comparable to many emerging-market fiat currencies during their peak monetary expansion years
Around 25% — Bitcoin's annual issuance was the same as a typical hyperinflationary fiat currency throughout 2024
questions.context: Post-April-2024-halving: 3.125 BTC per block × ~52,560 blocks/year ≈ 164,250 BTC/year. Divided by ~19.7M total ≈ 0.83%/year inflation. Gold's annual production is roughly 1.5% of above-ground stock. Bitcoin's monetary scarcity exceeded gold's for the first time.

questions.question: Bitcoin's proof-of-work requires miners to find a 'nonce' value such that a block's SHA-256 hash starts with a certain number of zeros. The probability of any single guess succeeding is extremely low. Why does this guess-and-check actually secure the network?
questions.answer: Rewriting history requires redoing all the work — an attacker needs more computing power than the rest combined
choices: Rewriting history requires redoing all the work — an attacker needs more computing power than the rest combined
Each guess is verified by a central authority — only the Bitcoin Foundation can authorize a valid hash for any block
The hash function ensures security — SHA-256 is mathematically impossible to compute backward in any way at all
Miners agree on a single answer — they vote among themselves before broadcasting any block to the global network
questions.context: Proof-of-work is what makes Bitcoin's history expensive to rewrite. To reverse a confirmed block, you must out-mine the rest of the network from that block forward — sustained 51%+ hashrate. This is the cost-imposition mechanism that makes the chain effectively immutable.

questions.question: Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment recalculates every 2,016 blocks — about every two weeks. The protocol targets an average block time of 10 minutes. If miners add hashrate, blocks come faster. What does the adjustment do?
questions.answer: Tunes the required leading zeros in the hash — making the puzzle harder or easier to keep block time near 10 minutes
choices: Tunes the required leading zeros in the hash — making the puzzle harder or easier to keep block time near 10 minutes
Changes the block reward — boosting the subsidy when hashrate falls, reducing it when hashrate rises substantially
Alters the maximum block size — adjusting capacity in response to network usage and transaction demand each cycle
Modifies the supply cap — raising 21 million slightly when hashrate is strong to incentivize continued network mining
questions.context: The 2,016-block window comes from 14 days × 24 hours × 6 blocks/hour = 2,016. The mechanism guarantees the issuance schedule regardless of how much hashrate is on the network. Supply policy stays unaffected even as hardware and energy costs change radically.

questions.question: Bitcoin uses SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm 256-bit) as its proof-of-work hashing function. SHA-256 was designed by the US NSA and standardized by NIST in 2001. Why was it a deliberate choice for Bitcoin?
questions.answer: Already battle-tested and broadly deployed — using established cryptography reduces the risk of subtle implementation bugs
choices: Already battle-tested and broadly deployed — using established cryptography reduces the risk of subtle implementation bugs
Designed for Bitcoin specifically — the NSA collaborated with Satoshi on a new hash function for cryptocurrency in 2008
Cheapest to compute — SHA-256 requires less electricity than competing hash functions for mining purposes nowadays
Patented — Satoshi licensed SHA-256 from the NSA to ensure exclusive rights for the Bitcoin network only
questions.context: SHA-256 was published in 2001 as part of the SHA-2 family. By 2008, it had survived years of public cryptanalysis. Bitcoin uses it twice in block hashing (sometimes called 'double SHA-256'). The choice reflects the cypherpunk discipline of using known-good primitives rather than novel ones.

questions.question: Bitcoin doesn't store account balances. Instead it tracks 'Unspent Transaction Outputs' (UTXOs). Every Bitcoin transaction consumes one or more UTXOs and produces new ones. What does this give Bitcoin?
questions.answer: Independent verifiability of each coin's history — parallel validation, simpler reasoning about double-spend prevention
choices: Independent verifiability of each coin's history — parallel validation, simpler reasoning about double-spend prevention
Single-number balances per user — UTXOs are added together at every block to update each wallet's balance figure
Built-in privacy for transactions — UTXOs hide the sender and receiver identities through built-in confidential addressing
Infinitely large blocks — UTXOs eliminate the need for any limit on the size of Bitcoin blocks at all
questions.context: The UTXO model treats each coin as a unique object with a provenance chain back to its block-subsidy origin. Ethereum, by contrast, uses an account-balance model. UTXO is more parallel-friendly and makes some kinds of analysis easier. Account models are simpler for some applications.

questions.question: A Bitcoin private key gives full control of the coins at its address. Lose the key, and the coins are unspendable forever. Estimates suggest 3-4 million BTC have been lost this way. How does this affect effective supply?
questions.answer: Effective circulating supply is below the 21M cap — lost coins are forever unreachable, making remaining BTC scarcer
choices: Effective circulating supply is below the 21M cap — lost coins are forever unreachable, making remaining BTC scarcer
Lost coins are reclaimed by the Bitcoin Foundation — and reissued to active addresses every halving cycle automatically
Lost coins have no effect — they remain on the blockchain and can be claimed by any address holder who finds them
Lost coins are mathematically destroyed — the protocol burns them after seven years of address inactivity by design
questions.context: Famous lost coins: James Howells's hard drive in a Newport landfill (~7,500 BTC), Stefan Thomas's 7,002 BTC behind a forgotten password. Estimates vary, but 3-4 million BTC are commonly cited as effectively lost. The deflationary effect compounds Bitcoin's already-fixed supply.

questions.question: Bitcoin transactions are signed using ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm) on the secp256k1 curve. A user proves they control an address by signing with their private key. What does the signature accomplish?
questions.answer: Proves knowledge of the key — verifiers can confirm authority to spend without ever seeing the secret itself
choices: Proves knowledge of the key — verifiers can confirm authority to spend without ever seeing the secret itself
Encrypts the transaction — the signature scrambles the recipient address so only the holder can decrypt it
Locks the funds for one year — ECDSA signatures impose a mandatory time-lock on every Bitcoin transaction made
Splits the key into shares — Bitcoin signatures require approval from at least three different parties on every transaction
questions.context: Public-key cryptography solves this problem: the signature can be verified using only the public key, but only someone with the private key could have produced it. This separates 'control of coins' from 'reveal of secret' — a fundamental property of cryptographic signature schemes.

questions.question: A Bitcoin 'multisig' address requires multiple signatures to spend. A common pattern is '2-of-3' — three keys exist, any two must sign. What practical properties does multisig enable?
questions.answer: Loss of any single key is recoverable, no single party can spend alone — used for treasuries, exchanges, custody
choices: Loss of any single key is recoverable, no single party can spend alone — used for treasuries, exchanges, custody
Bitcoin must be sent through Coinbase or another major exchange to use multisig — it cannot work peer-to-peer ever
Multisig is only used by governments — the Bitcoin protocol restricts multisig functionality to state-level signers only
Multisig doubles the fee per transaction — there are no other practical or security benefits beyond the higher cost
questions.context: Multisig replaces single-point-of-failure custody. Major exchanges, family offices, and corporate treasuries use multisig schemes (often 2-of-3 or 3-of-5) to require multiple signatures, geographically distribute keys, and enable governance over Bitcoin holdings.

questions.question: Bitcoin mining hardware has evolved through three generations: CPU mining (2009-10), GPU mining (2010-13), ASIC mining (2013-present). ASICs are chips designed to do nothing but Bitcoin hashing. Why did they come to dominate?
questions.answer: Specialization wins — an ASIC's energy-per-hash is thousands of times better than general-purpose CPUs or GPUs
choices: Specialization wins — an ASIC's energy-per-hash is thousands of times better than general-purpose CPUs or GPUs
ASICs were mandated by the protocol — Bitcoin Core released a 2013 update requiring ASIC mining hardware specifically
ASICs are cheaper to buy — a typical mining ASIC costs about $50 while a GPU rig costs about $5,000 to assemble
ASICs are easier to program — most miners lack the skills to operate the older GPU-based mining software systems
questions.context: Bitmain's Antminer line, MicroBT's Whatsminer, and others dominate today's mining market. The specialization is so extreme ASICs are useless for any other task. This is both Bitcoin's incredible security budget and the source of ongoing debates about hashrate centralization.

questions.question: Bitcoin's block-size limit was originally 1 MB. After the 'block-size wars' of 2015-2017, the network activated SegWit in August 2017, effectively raising capacity. What does SegWit do, technically?
questions.answer: Moves signature data out of the main transaction body — fitting more transactions in the same block weight budget
choices: Moves signature data out of the main transaction body — fitting more transactions in the same block weight budget
Removes the block size limit entirely — Bitcoin blocks could be unlimited size after the August 2017 upgrade
Outsources verification to third parties — SegWit transactions are validated by trusted hubs rather than by full nodes
Compresses transactions through machine learning — SegWit applies neural-network compression to block contents
questions.context: SegWit's full name: Segregated Witness. By treating signature ('witness') data as discounted weight, it allowed more transactions per block without raising the headline 1 MB limit. The block-size wars produced the Bitcoin Cash fork (BCH) by those who wanted larger raw blocks instead.

questions.question: On November 14, 2021, at block 709,632, Bitcoin activated the Taproot upgrade. Taproot was the largest protocol upgrade since SegWit. What does Taproot enable, in plain terms?
questions.answer: Smarter, more private, more compact transactions — complex spending conditions can look identical to simple ones on-chain
choices: Smarter, more private, more compact transactions — complex spending conditions can look identical to simple ones on-chain
Faster block times across the network — Taproot reduced Bitcoin's target block interval from 10 minutes to 5 minutes
Higher supply cap of new coins — Taproot raised the maximum BTC supply from 21 million to 23 million at activation
Quantum resistance against attacks — Taproot replaced ECDSA with a post-quantum signature scheme for all transactions
questions.context: Taproot combined Schnorr signatures, MAST (Merkelized Abstract Syntax Trees), and Tapscript. The result: smart-contract-like spending conditions can be hidden until execution, all complex transactions look like simple ones, and signature aggregation enables more efficient multisig. Activation: block 709,632.

questions.question: Mt. Gox — based in Tokyo, run by Mark Karpelès — was the largest Bitcoin exchange by 2013, handling ~70% of global trades. In February 2014 the exchange suspended withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy. How many BTC went missing?
questions.answer: About 850,000 BTC — most belonged to customers, with the exchange having no funds to make them whole
choices: About 850,000 BTC — most belonged to customers, with the exchange having no funds to make them whole
About 100,000 BTC — a minor incident at the time involving only the exchange's own treasury holdings briefly
About 5,000,000 BTC — exceeding the total Bitcoin mined to that date, a clear sign of massive accounting fraud
About 21,000 BTC — exactly matching one one-thousandth of the entire eventual supply of Bitcoin at the cap
questions.context: Mt. Gox's collapse exposed catastrophic custody and security failures. Karpelès was later convicted on related charges. Some BTC was recovered (~140K BTC); creditor distributions began in 2024 — a decade later. The collapse remains the canonical example of exchange custody risk.

questions.question: On November 8, 2022, FTX — then the second-largest crypto exchange — froze withdrawals. Founder Sam Bankman-Fried had moved customer funds to his trading firm Alameda. About $8B was missing. SBF was sentenced in March 2024. What sentence?
questions.answer: 25 years in federal prison — for wire fraud, conspiracy, and money laundering charges related to the collapse
choices: 25 years in federal prison — for wire fraud, conspiracy, and money laundering charges related to the collapse
5 years in federal prison — reduced sentence after SBF agreed to cooperate with US Department of Justice investigators
Probation only — given his charitable giving and effective-altruism background, the court declined to impose prison time
Death penalty — SBF was the first US executive ever to face capital punishment for financial fraud at the federal level
questions.context: SBF was convicted on all seven counts in November 2023; sentenced March 28, 2024 to 25 years by Judge Lewis Kaplan in the Southern District of New York. He had been a major Democratic donor and a prominent figure in 'effective altruism' fundraising. The FTX case is the canonical example of exchange-custody risk.

questions.question: In May 2022, the Terra/Luna ecosystem collapsed in a matter of days. Terra was an 'algorithmic stablecoin' promising a $1 peg; Luna was its governance token. About $60 billion vanished. What does this illustrate about Bitcoin vs 'crypto'?
questions.answer: Algorithmic stablecoins are NOT Bitcoin — they require active management and can collapse; Bitcoin has no such dependency
choices: Algorithmic stablecoins are NOT Bitcoin — they require active management and can collapse; Bitcoin has no such dependency
All crypto is fraudulent uniformly — Terra's collapse proves no digital asset can be trusted under any conditions
Terra was actually a Bitcoin product — and its failure was caused by errors in the Bitcoin Core software itself
Algorithmic stablecoins are stronger than Bitcoin — Terra's collapse was caused by a coordinated short-seller attack
questions.context: Terra's founder Do Kwon was extradited and faced charges in multiple jurisdictions. The 'algorithmic' peg mechanism worked only as long as confidence held; once it broke, the death spiral was rapid. Bitcoin's design has no comparable failure mode — no peg to defend, no governance token to inflate.

questions.question: In May 2021, China formally banned Bitcoin mining. About 50% of global hashrate went offline within weeks. Many predicted Bitcoin would collapse without Chinese miners. Instead, hashrate recovered within months. What does this episode demonstrate?
questions.answer: Bitcoin's decentralization works — mining migrated to the US, Kazakhstan, Russia; the protocol survived a 50% shock
choices: Bitcoin's decentralization works — mining migrated to the US, Kazakhstan, Russia; the protocol survived a 50% shock
Bitcoin's centralization was exposed — the network barely survived and required emergency intervention from Bitcoin Core
China's ban was reversed quickly — the People's Bank of China reinstated Bitcoin mining within months after the ban
Hashrate is irrelevant to security — Bitcoin depends entirely on the supply cap rather than on any mining activity
questions.context: Pre-ban, China hosted an estimated 65-75% of global hashrate. By mid-2022, the US became the top hashrate jurisdiction, followed by Kazakhstan and Russia. The difficulty adjustment did exactly what it was designed to do — easier puzzles let remaining miners produce blocks at target rate.

questions.question: On September 7, 2021, El Salvador became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender. President Nayib Bukele led the move. Citizens received $30 in BTC through the government's Chivo wallet at launch. What broader significance?
questions.answer: Sovereign-state proof of concept — Bitcoin could legally function as money at the national level under real conditions
choices: Sovereign-state proof of concept — Bitcoin could legally function as money at the national level under real conditions
Complete failure of the experiment — Bukele revoked Bitcoin's legal-tender status within months of the September launch
Chinese geopolitical plot — the Salvadoran adoption was secretly funded by Beijing to undermine the US dollar abroad
Forced action by the IMF — international financial institutions had pressured Bukele to adopt Bitcoin against his wishes
questions.context: Adoption among ordinary Salvadorans has been mixed; Chivo had technical problems; the IMF objected. But the precedent stands: a sovereign nation made Bitcoin legal tender, accumulated reserves, and continues to hold them. The country's later economic recovery has been partly attributed to the move.

questions.question: Mt. Gox, FTX, Celsius (2022), Voyager (2022), BlockFi (2022), Genesis (2023) — all centralized custodians where users gave up control of their private keys. What single phrase captures the lesson Bitcoiners drew?
questions.answer: Not your keys, not your coins — if you don't hold the private key, you don't actually own the Bitcoin in question
choices: Not your keys, not your coins — if you don't hold the private key, you don't actually own the Bitcoin in question
Buy and hold forever no matter what — Bitcoiners learned that no exchange should ever be used for any purpose at any time
Trust the auditors and CPAs — third-party verification can fully replace direct custody for sophisticated holders going forward
Government regulation is needed — exchanges should be nationalized to prevent any future custody failure event happening
questions.context: 'Not your keys, not your coins' became the Bitcoin community's mantra after each successive exchange failure. The phrase is attributed to Andreas Antonopoulos, who used it in talks and his book 'Mastering Bitcoin' (2014). Self-custody — holding your own keys — is the canonical safe pattern.

questions.question: Bitcoin custody sits on a spectrum: full self-custody with a hardware wallet at one end; leaving coins on an exchange at the other. What's the trade-off the spectrum captures?
questions.answer: Self-custody trades convenience for sovereignty — exchanges trade sovereignty for convenience, and lose coins in failures
choices: Self-custody trades convenience for sovereignty — exchanges trade sovereignty for convenience, and lose coins in failures
Self-custody is illegal in most jurisdictions — modern regulations require all Bitcoin to be held through licensed exchanges
Self-custody is identical to exchanges — there is no practical difference between the two custody models in any way
Self-custody is mandated by Bitcoin Core — the protocol prohibits exchange custody and enforces individual key holding
questions.context: Hardware wallets (Ledger, Trezor, Coldcard) keep private keys in secure devices that never expose them to internet-connected computers. The trade-off — convenience vs control — is real. Each user makes the choice; the broader principle is that exchange custody is fundamentally different from self-custody.

questions.question: Bitcoin's 2017 'block-size wars' produced a hard fork in August 2017. A subset of the community split off to create a new chain with larger blocks. What was that chain called?
questions.answer: Bitcoin Cash (BCH) — diverged from Bitcoin at block 478,558 to enable 8 MB blocks initially after the split
choices: Bitcoin Cash (BCH) — diverged from Bitcoin at block 478,558 to enable 8 MB blocks initially after the split
Bitcoin Classic — diverged at block 100,000 to enforce smaller blocks for greater decentralization purposes
Bitcoin Diamond — diverged at the time of the 2024 halving to introduce gold-backed unit conversions
Bitcoin Crystal — diverged in 2023 to add a Proof-of-Stake consensus mechanism replacing original Proof-of-Work
questions.context: Bitcoin Cash forked on August 1, 2017, at block 478,558. The block-size debate split the community over whether to scale on-chain (raise block size) or off-chain (Lightning Network and SegWit). The surviving Bitcoin chain (BTC) chose off-chain scaling; BCH chose larger blocks.

questions.question: The Lightning Network is a second-layer scaling solution for Bitcoin. The white paper, by Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja, was published in 2015. What problem does Lightning aim to solve?
questions.answer: On-chain throughput limits — Lightning enables instant, low-fee payments off-chain, settled to Bitcoin in batches
choices: On-chain throughput limits — Lightning enables instant, low-fee payments off-chain, settled to Bitcoin in batches
Mining centralization in pools — Lightning replaces SHA-256 proof-of-work with a fairer distribution mechanism
Supply cap rigidity in the protocol — Lightning allows the 21 million cap to flex temporarily during high-demand periods
Privacy weakness on the main chain — Lightning encrypts all on-chain Bitcoin transactions to hide sender and recipient
questions.context: The Poon-Dryja paper introduced bidirectional payment channels and a network of them. Lightning lets parties transact off-chain, settling to Bitcoin only when a channel closes. The result: instant, fee-cheap micropayments while preserving Bitcoin's base-layer security and 21M cap.

questions.question: The Lightning Network mainnet launched in January 2018 on Bitcoin. By 2024 the network had grown to thousands of nodes with significant total channel capacity. What's the mechanism that makes Lightning trust-minimized?
questions.answer: Payment channels are secured by Bitcoin's base layer — disputes are resolved on-chain if any party tries to cheat
choices: Payment channels are secured by Bitcoin's base layer — disputes are resolved on-chain if any party tries to cheat
Lightning relies on trusted node operators — all transactions are verified by a small group of approved Lightning operators
Lightning uses a separate token — payments inside the network do not interact with Bitcoin at all in any way ever
Lightning is fully on-chain — every Lightning payment is recorded as a full transaction on the Bitcoin main chain
questions.context: Lightning's security model uses 'punishment' transactions: if a counterparty broadcasts an old channel state to steal funds, the honest party can broadcast a counter-transaction that takes ALL the channel funds. Cheating is economically irrational. The base layer guarantees enforcement.

questions.question: Lightning payments are routed through a graph of payment channels — each hop forwards a payment to the next. What's the cryptographic primitive that ensures each hop is honest about forwarding?
questions.answer: Hash Time-Locked Contracts (HTLCs) — payments commit to a hash; revealing the preimage releases funds at each hop
choices: Hash Time-Locked Contracts (HTLCs) — payments commit to a hash; revealing the preimage releases funds at each hop
Trusted intermediaries — Lightning hubs are vetted by the Bitcoin Foundation and audited weekly by Lightning Labs staff
Mining work at each hop — each Lightning hop requires a small proof-of-work payment to deter dishonest routing decisions
Government registries of payments — Lightning payments are recorded in a US Treasury database all participants consult
questions.context: HTLCs let payments be sent through multiple hops atomically: either every hop completes, or none do. The hash-preimage mechanism ensures that no intermediate node can take the money without forwarding. The recipient's reveal of the preimage cascades back, completing the chain of payments.

questions.question: Compared to base-layer Bitcoin transactions, Lightning Network payments have very different characteristics on fees and confirmation times. What's the practical difference for everyday use?
questions.answer: Lightning settles in seconds with fees of cents or less — base-layer Bitcoin can take minutes and cost dollars in fees
choices: Lightning settles in seconds with fees of cents or less — base-layer Bitcoin can take minutes and cost dollars in fees
Lightning settles in days with very high fees — base-layer Bitcoin is faster and cheaper for any small payment use
Lightning and base-layer Bitcoin are identical — there is no practical or technical difference in fees or time at all
Lightning settles in years at most — payments are only finalized at the end of each Bitcoin halving epoch by default
questions.context: Lightning enables economic models that base-layer Bitcoin cannot support: streaming sats per minute (podcasting 2.0), micropayments for content, retail point-of-sale. El Salvador's Chivo wallet supports Lightning. Strike, Cash App, and various Bitcoin-native apps integrate it natively.

questions.question: Lightning Network represents a particular vision of how Bitcoin scales. Rather than making the base layer process millions of transactions per second, base layer handles settlement only. What analogy maps onto this?
questions.answer: Like a banking system — Bitcoin base is the central settlement layer; Lightning is the retail-payment rails on top
choices: Like a banking system — Bitcoin base is the central settlement layer; Lightning is the retail-payment rails on top
Like a movie streaming service — Lightning is the streaming layer while base layer Bitcoin is a separate movie archive
Like a kitchen pantry storage — base layer Bitcoin stores food while Lightning prepares each meal as ordered each time
Like an interstate highway — base layer Bitcoin moves slowly while Lightning enables high-speed parallel transport modes
questions.context: Nik Bhatia's 'Layered Money' (2021) develops this layered analogy carefully. Historically, gold settled between banks while banknotes circulated for commerce. Bitcoin/Lightning recreates this pattern in digital form: base-layer Bitcoin for final settlement, Lightning for commerce.

questions.question: Bitcoin's intellectual lineage runs through the cypherpunk mailing list (1992-2010s). David Chaum's DigiCash launched in 1989 but went bankrupt in 1998. What was DigiCash's critical limitation that Bitcoin overcame?
questions.answer: DigiCash required a central issuer — Chaum's mint could be subpoenaed, regulated, or shut down, and ultimately was
choices: DigiCash required a central issuer — Chaum's mint could be subpoenaed, regulated, or shut down, and ultimately was
DigiCash had a small supply — Chaum's currency was capped at one million units, smaller than Bitcoin's design allows
DigiCash was too fast for banks — banks couldn't process the high transaction speed and refused to participate in the system
DigiCash had no encryption — Chaum's design exposed user transactions to public view in the original implementation
questions.context: DigiCash had genuinely innovative cryptography (blind signatures) but a fatal architectural flaw: it needed a central mint. When the mint failed, the system failed. Bitcoin's combination of public ledger + proof-of-work eliminated the need for a central issuer — the breakthrough Chaum couldn't make.

questions.question: Adam Back's Hashcash (1997) was originally designed not as money but as an anti-spam measure for email. Senders had to compute a small proof-of-work for each email. What innovation did Hashcash introduce that Bitcoin later inherited?
questions.answer: Proof-of-work — using costly computation as verifiable proof that resources were spent, deterring spam or attack
choices: Proof-of-work — using costly computation as verifiable proof that resources were spent, deterring spam or attack
Public-key cryptography — Hashcash pioneered RSA-style signatures used in modern Bitcoin transactions to this day
Distributed consensus algorithms — Hashcash implemented a working version of Byzantine fault tolerance for the first time
Hardware acceleration techniques — Hashcash was the first system designed to be mined using specialized ASIC chips at scale
questions.context: Adam Back is cited in the Bitcoin white paper. He went on to co-found Blockstream and is a major figure in Bitcoin research and development. The Hashcash proof-of-work design — make-the-attacker-pay-CPU-cost — was directly adapted by Satoshi for Bitcoin's mining.

questions.question: Wei Dai's 'b-money' (1998) was a thought experiment, not a working system. Posted to the cypherpunk mailing list, it described a hypothetical digital cash with features Bitcoin later implemented. What did b-money propose?
questions.answer: A distributed ledger maintained by all participants — no central mint — but couldn't fully solve double-spend itself
choices: A distributed ledger maintained by all participants — no central mint — but couldn't fully solve double-spend itself
A centralized mint backed by gold — Dai's design closely resembled Chaum's earlier DigiCash architecture exactly today
A government-issued digital currency — Dai proposed that the US Treasury should issue b-money directly to all citizens
A patent-protected payment system — Dai planned to license b-money commercially to banks and corporations widely
questions.context: Satoshi cited Wei Dai in early Bitcoin emails as an inspiration. The b-money paper outlined the basic vision: a distributed system with no central issuer. The specific mechanism (proof-of-work + public ledger) was Satoshi's contribution that made Dai's vision actually work in practice.

questions.question: Nick Szabo's 'bit gold' (2005) was the closest pre-Bitcoin design — a chain of cryptographic puzzles whose solutions could be verified and timestamped. Szabo published years before Bitcoin appeared. Why is he rumored to be Satoshi?
questions.answer: Writing style and technical interests match Satoshi's — and bit gold's design overlaps with Bitcoin's substantially
choices: Writing style and technical interests match Satoshi's — and bit gold's design overlaps with Bitcoin's substantially
He confessed publicly in 2017 — Szabo revealed himself as Satoshi at the New York Consensus Conference that year
His Microsoft email account leaked — Szabo's role at Microsoft became the basis for the Satoshi attribution by 2015
His tax returns proved it definitively — IRS subpoenaed records that conclusively identified Szabo as Satoshi in 2019
questions.context: Szabo has consistently denied being Satoshi. The case rests on circumstantial evidence: writing style, areas of expertise, his prior bit-gold design. There's no proof. Other candidates have included Hal Finney and Adam Back. The community largely accepts Satoshi's identity will likely never be confirmed.

questions.question: Bitcoin is often called a 'fair launch' — distinct from later projects with pre-mines, founder allocations, ICOs, or VC token allotments. What does 'fair launch' mean concretely for Bitcoin?
questions.answer: No coins existed before Genesis, no founder reserve — everyone competed equally for early blocks at the launch
choices: No coins existed before Genesis, no founder reserve — everyone competed equally for early blocks at the launch
Satoshi received exactly 50% — and distributed the remainder to founding contributors before the network's first block ever
The Bitcoin Foundation pre-allocated coins — early developers and investors received millions of BTC before Genesis fully
The US government received 20% of supply — as part of a quiet arrangement with Satoshi before the network's public launch
questions.context: Bitcoin's fair launch is one of its most distinctive properties. Ethereum had a pre-sale; many alt-coins are heavily allocated to insiders before public launch. Bitcoin's mining began at block 1 with no prior issuance. Any coins Satoshi mined were earned by running the software when it was free.

questions.question: Bitcoin has no CEO, no board, no foundation controlling protocol changes, and no central legal entity. The Bitcoin Foundation existed briefly (2012-2015) but never controlled the protocol. Why is this absence load-bearing?
questions.answer: A leaderless protocol cannot be coerced — no founder or entity to subpoena, sue, sanction, or politically pressure
choices: A leaderless protocol cannot be coerced — no founder or entity to subpoena, sue, sanction, or politically pressure
Bitcoin is informal in nature — without a corporate structure, the network is a hobby project with limited oversight
Bitcoin will collapse over time — without a foundation to maintain it, the protocol cannot survive future upgrades
Bitcoin is purely speculative — its value comes from greater-fool dynamics rather than from any real monetary use
questions.context: Compare to Ethereum (Vitalik Buterin + Ethereum Foundation), Solana (Solana Labs + Solana Foundation), Ripple (Ripple Labs). Each has a clear point of failure for regulators or attackers. Bitcoin's protocol is maintained by a loose community of developers across multiple implementations.

questions.question: Bitcoin's protocol upgrades happen by social consensus, not corporate decree. A proposed change becomes a BIP (Bitcoin Improvement Proposal); it must gain support across developers, miners, nodes, users. What does the process protect against?
questions.answer: Top-down protocol changes — no single party can alter Bitcoin without convincing the broader network to upgrade
choices: Top-down protocol changes — no single party can alter Bitcoin without convincing the broader network to upgrade
All bug fixes generally — the BIP process specifically prohibits any change that fixes security flaws in the code
All performance gains — Bitcoin's process makes it impossible to improve the protocol's speed or efficiency at all
Decentralization itself — BIP-driven changes always centralize more power into the Bitcoin Core development team
questions.context: The BIP process produces slow, conservative, deliberate change — by design. SegWit took years of debate; Taproot took longer. The friction is a feature: it makes Bitcoin resistant to capture by any single developer faction, mining pool, or corporate sponsor. Stability is part of sound money.

questions.question: Bitcoin is often described as 'digital gold.' Gold has been the historical sound-money standard for thousands of years. What property does Bitcoin claim to share with gold — and where does it exceed gold?
questions.answer: Both are scarce and durable — but Bitcoin's supply is fixed at 21M while gold's increases ~1.5% per year still
choices: Both are scarce and durable — but Bitcoin's supply is fixed at 21M while gold's increases ~1.5% per year still
Both are heavy metals at base — but Bitcoin weighs less and ships easier through international supply chains and customs
Both are mined with shovels — Bitcoin uses physical mining equipment indistinguishable from traditional gold mining
Both are issued by central banks — gold by the US Treasury and Bitcoin by the People's Bank of China since 2018
questions.context: The 'digital gold' frame compares stocks-and-flows. Gold's stock-to-flow ratio is around 60 (60 years of current production to reach existing stock). Bitcoin's stock-to-flow exceeded gold's after the April 2024 halving and will continue to rise with each future halving.

questions.question: In January 2024 the SEC approved spot Bitcoin ETFs in the US. BlackRock's IBIT and Fidelity's FBTC began trading. These products let investors gain Bitcoin exposure through brokerage accounts. Why was this significant?
questions.answer: Legitimized Bitcoin in US capital markets — major asset managers could now hold Bitcoin within standard structures
choices: Legitimized Bitcoin in US capital markets — major asset managers could now hold Bitcoin within standard structures
Nationalized Bitcoin into government — the SEC took control of the protocol after January 2024 and began regulating blocks
Capped Bitcoin's price by regulation — the ETF approval came with a regulatory ceiling on how high Bitcoin could trade
Eliminated self-custody by law — after January 2024, holding Bitcoin outside an SEC-approved ETF became illegal in the US
questions.context: Spot Bitcoin ETFs accumulated tens of billions in assets within their first year. They represent a one-way flow into Bitcoin from traditional finance. The 11-year SEC battle over approval (Winklevoss twins first filed in 2013) ended with court rulings forcing the SEC's hand. Self-custody remains fully available.

questions.question: MicroStrategy (now 'Strategy'), a US business intelligence firm, began converting its corporate treasury to Bitcoin in August 2020 under CEO Michael Saylor. By late 2024 the company held over 250,000 BTC. Why has this been influential?
questions.answer: Demonstrated a public company could substitute Bitcoin for cash on balance sheet — surviving multiple drawdown cycles
choices: Demonstrated a public company could substitute Bitcoin for cash on balance sheet — surviving multiple drawdown cycles
Crashed into bankruptcy — MicroStrategy declared bankruptcy in 2022 after Bitcoin's price decline destroyed it fully
Was forced by SEC regulators — MicroStrategy was required by the agency to hold Bitcoin instead of dollars as sanction
Targeted retail investors directly — MicroStrategy sold Bitcoin to small investors at a markup as primary business
questions.context: MicroStrategy's August 2020 announcement converted its first $250 million in treasury reserves to Bitcoin. The strategy survived the 2021-2022 drawdown and accelerated through 2024. Other public companies (Block, Tesla briefly, GameStop in 2025) followed. The pattern demonstrates Bitcoin as a corporate-treasury asset.

questions.question: Bitcoin's electricity use has been heavily criticized. Estimates put Bitcoin mining at ~0.5% of global electricity. Defenders argue this critique misses what Bitcoin's energy use accomplishes. What's the standard rebuttal?
questions.answer: Energy buys security and credible neutrality — sound money has real costs, like gold mining historically
choices: Energy buys security and credible neutrality — sound money has real costs, like gold mining historically
Bitcoin uses no energy at all — the critique is based on fabricated estimates; the network runs on tiny solar panels
Energy use is fully offset by miners — Bitcoin mining generates electricity through built-in wind turbines at each rig
Energy use is irrelevant to outcomes — the SEC approval in 2024 exempted Bitcoin from environmental concerns by law
questions.context: The energy-use debate is the most common environmental critique of Bitcoin. Defenders point out: (1) gold mining uses comparable or more energy; (2) traditional banking infrastructure uses substantial energy; (3) increasingly, Bitcoin mining uses stranded or excess renewable energy (hydro, wind, flare gas).

questions.question: Bitcoin is sometimes confused with 'crypto' — an umbrella term covering Ethereum, Solana, Ripple, and thousands of other tokens. Bitcoiners argue these aren't the same thing. What's the substantive distinction?
questions.answer: Bitcoin has fair launch + no founder + fixed supply + leaderless protocol — most other tokens have none of these properties
choices: Bitcoin has fair launch + no founder + fixed supply + leaderless protocol — most other tokens have none of these properties
Bitcoin is the same as all crypto — there is no meaningful distinction between Bitcoin and any other token whatsoever
Bitcoin is simply older than the rest — the only difference is that Bitcoin launched in 2009 while other tokens launched later
Bitcoin is government-backed by treaties — and all other tokens are private, which is the only relevant difference between them
questions.context: The economic and structural distinctions are substantive: Bitcoin has no pre-mine, no foundation that controls the protocol, no governance token, no CEO, no marketing budget. Most other tokens have one or more of these. Lumping Bitcoin with FTX-listed altcoins obscures these differences.

questions.question: Bitcoin advocates often cite Saifedean Ammous ('The Bitcoin Standard' 2018), Nik Bhatia ('Layered Money' 2021), Jeff Booth ('The Price of Tomorrow' 2020). These books make a broader claim about Bitcoin. What's the unifying argument?
questions.answer: Bitcoin is sound money in digital form — returning the world to a hard-money standard fiat had displaced since 1971
choices: Bitcoin is sound money in digital form — returning the world to a hard-money standard fiat had displaced since 1971
Bitcoin will replace stocks soon — these authors argue all equity markets should be denominated in Bitcoin by 2030 at latest
Bitcoin is government-friendly always — these authors argue that central banks should adopt Bitcoin as the new world reserve
Bitcoin is purely speculative still — these authors argue Bitcoin has no actual monetary properties beyond price action
questions.context: The Bitcoin-as-sound-money framing connects directly to Austrian economics: Mises on calculation, Hayek on knowledge, Rothbard on hard money, Bastiat on what fiat money hides. The 1971 Nixon shock ended the last formal gold-dollar link. Bitcoin's 2009 launch is positioned as the return.

questions.question: A Bitcoin transaction is broadcast to the network but isn't yet confirmed. Where does it sit while waiting for a miner to include it in a block?
questions.answer: In the mempool — a global pool of pending transactions, each waiting for miners to include them in the next block
choices: In the mempool — a global pool of pending transactions, each waiting for miners to include them in the next block
In the Bitcoin Foundation queue — a centralized list maintained by Bitcoin Core developers in San Francisco currently
In the user's wallet alone — pending transactions are stored only locally until the recipient comes back online to claim
In the SEC's federal database — pending transactions must be approved by US regulators before any miner can include them
questions.context: Each Bitcoin node maintains its own mempool — a set of unconfirmed transactions it has seen and validated. Miners pick from their mempool to build candidate blocks, generally prioritizing higher-fee transactions. The mempool is not a single global object — each node has its own — but they're typically very similar.

questions.question: A Bitcoin wallet's 'seed phrase' is a sequence of 12 or 24 English words from the BIP39 standard (2013). The seed phrase is the master key. Why is the seed phrase so dangerous to store carelessly?
questions.answer: It is the master key — anyone with the phrase can recreate the full wallet and spend all funds in any derived address
choices: It is the master key — anyone with the phrase can recreate the full wallet and spend all funds in any derived address
It expires after one year automatically — wallets must regenerate seed phrases annually or the funds become permanently locked
It must be shared with Coinbase — exchanges require seed phrases from all users for ongoing regulatory compliance work
It is encrypted with the user's birthday — seed phrases require a date of birth combination to function correctly in wallets
questions.context: BIP39 lets users back up an entire wallet in 12 or 24 words from a fixed wordlist. The phrase deterministically generates all the private keys. Storage best practices: never type into a connected device; etch into metal for fire resistance; geographic separation. Mistakes here are unrecoverable.

questions.question: Bitcoin mining pools combine the hashrate of many individual miners — sharing rewards proportionally. Pools like Foundry USA, Antpool, F2Pool dominate hashrate share. Why does this raise centralization concerns?
questions.answer: Pool operators choose which transactions to include — concentrated pool control could affect censorship resistance
choices: Pool operators choose which transactions to include — concentrated pool control could affect censorship resistance
Pool operators print new BTC — pools have authority to expand Bitcoin's 21M supply through internal governance votes
Pool operators set the global price — Bitcoin's USD price is determined daily by agreement among major mining pools
Pool operators control difficulty — the protocol delegates difficulty adjustment to whichever pool has the largest share
questions.context: Pool centralization is a legitimate concern even though it can't change the supply cap. If one pool got over 51% hashrate sustainably, it could theoretically reorganize chain or censor transactions. Individual miners can switch pools quickly. Stratum V2 and other tools aim to reduce pool operators' transaction-selection power.

questions.question: Bitcoin's Taproot upgrade (November 2021) introduced Schnorr signatures, replacing ECDSA for some uses. Schnorr signatures have advantages. What's the key advantage relevant to multisig?
questions.answer: Signatures from multiple parties can be aggregated into one — making large multisig look like single-key spends on-chain
choices: Signatures from multiple parties can be aggregated into one — making large multisig look like single-key spends on-chain
Schnorr signatures are exactly one byte — they save 99% of transaction space compared to ECDSA in every scenario actually
Schnorr signatures are mandatory by code — after November 2021, all Bitcoin transactions must use Schnorr instead of ECDSA
Schnorr signatures are unbreakable mathematically — they cannot be forged even by quantum computers of any future size
questions.context: Schnorr's linearity property enables signature aggregation. A 5-of-7 multisig can produce a single combined signature, indistinguishable from a single-key spend on-chain. This improves both privacy (multisig setups don't reveal themselves) and efficiency. MuSig2 is a current protocol for safely aggregating Schnorr signatures.

questions.question: A 'full node' is software that downloads, validates, and stores the entire Bitcoin blockchain. Anyone can run one — it requires ordinary hardware and internet access. What does running your own give you?
questions.answer: Independent verification of consensus rules — your node enforces the supply cap and rules without trusting any third party
choices: Independent verification of consensus rules — your node enforces the supply cap and rules without trusting any third party
Mining rewards directly per block — running a full node earns the operator a share of the block subsidy proportional to uptime
Exchange discounts on fees — node operators get reduced fees at major exchanges as a reward for supporting the network
Government subsidy payments — running a node qualifies the operator for tax breaks in most developed countries by 2024
questions.context: Full nodes are how Bitcoin's consensus rules are enforced. Each node independently checks every transaction and block. If a miner tried to issue 51 BTC in a coinbase, every full node would reject the block as invalid. The decentralization of node operation is what makes Bitcoin's rules unfalsifiable.

questions.question: After the SEC approved spot Bitcoin ETFs in January 2024, BlackRock's IBIT became one of the fastest-growing ETFs in history, reaching over $10B in months. What does this institutional flow tell us?
questions.answer: Large pools of traditional capital had been waiting for regulatory clearance — and chose to allocate quickly once approved
choices: Large pools of traditional capital had been waiting for regulatory clearance — and chose to allocate quickly once approved
BlackRock now controls Bitcoin entirely — the firm acquired a majority stake in the protocol through ETF purchases in 2024
Bitcoin became fully regulated daily — after the ETF approval, the SEC requires direct oversight of every Bitcoin transaction
Bitcoin was nationalized to government — BlackRock's ETF effectively transferred Bitcoin's protocol governance to the Treasury
questions.context: IBIT and FBTC accumulated billions in assets within their first months. The flow demonstrates pent-up demand from advisors, family offices, and institutional allocators who could not previously access Bitcoin within standard mandates. The protocol itself is unchanged; ETFs are wrappers around BTC.

questions.question: Bitcoin transactions pay fees to miners. After the 2024 halving cut the block subsidy in half, fees became a larger share of miner revenue. What's the long-term implication for Bitcoin's economic model?
questions.answer: By 2140 miners earn from fees only — a thriving block-space market is essential for continued network security long-term
choices: By 2140 miners earn from fees only — a thriving block-space market is essential for continued network security long-term
By 2140 miners are replaced by AI — automated trading bots will handle all Bitcoin transaction processing after the cap is hit
By 2140 the protocol restarts itself — the Bitcoin Foundation will reset block subsidies to 50 BTC and begin again from zero
By 2140 mining becomes free entirely — the protocol will subsidize all miners directly from the US Federal Reserve budget
questions.context: The fee market is Bitcoin's long-term security budget. As the subsidy declines, sustained fee demand becomes essential. Block-space demand depends on usage patterns: ETF arbitrage, Ordinals, Lightning channel opens, sovereign reserves. Whether this will sustain miners is an active research question.

questions.question: In 2023 a new use of Bitcoin emerged: 'Ordinals' and 'Inscriptions' — using the blockchain to embed data into individual satoshis. Casey Rodarmor's system, launched January 2023, became controversial. Why?
questions.answer: Increased block-space competition and fees — some welcomed the revenue, others objected to non-monetary uses of base layer
choices: Increased block-space competition and fees — some welcomed the revenue, others objected to non-monetary uses of base layer
Was a serious security flaw — Ordinals exposed a critical bug that allowed attackers to forge Bitcoin transactions on demand
Froze the entire network — Ordinals slowed Bitcoin's confirmation times to weeks during early 2023 across major full nodes
Violated the supply cap rules — Ordinals issued additional Bitcoin beyond the 21 million programmed maximum supply count
questions.context: Ordinals turned Bitcoin block space into a market for digital collectibles. Fees rose substantially; miner revenue benefited; some users complained that on-chain data inflated UTXO sets and crowded out monetary use. The debate continues: is Bitcoin only money, or is paying real fees for other purposes a legitimate market signal?

questions.question: Bitcoin addresses come in several formats. Originally addresses began with '1' (Legacy P2PKH). SegWit added 'bc1' addresses. Taproot added 'bc1p' addresses. Why does Bitcoin support multiple formats simultaneously?
questions.answer: Backward compatibility across upgrades — old addresses still work; new formats enable features without breaking wallets
choices: Backward compatibility across upgrades — old addresses still work; new formats enable features without breaking wallets
Geographic restriction by regulation — different address formats are required in different countries by national law
Tax categorization rules — the US IRS requires different formats for capital gains versus ordinary income transactions
Mining priority routing — newer address formats get priority confirmation by miners ahead of legacy address transactions
questions.context: The address-format evolution mirrors Bitcoin's soft-fork upgrades. Legacy '1...' addresses still work and are still accepted; SegWit 'bc1q...' is more efficient; Taproot 'bc1p...' unlocks Schnorr aggregation. Bitcoin's commitment to backward compatibility means old wallets keep working even as the protocol gains capability.

questions.question: Bitcoin mining increasingly uses energy that would otherwise be wasted: flared natural gas at oil wells, stranded hydropower with no grid connection, off-peak excess renewables. What does this energy pattern undercut?
questions.answer: The 'wasteful energy' critique — Bitcoin often consumes energy that has no other economic use and would otherwise be discarded
choices: The 'wasteful energy' critique — Bitcoin often consumes energy that has no other economic use and would otherwise be discarded
The 'sound money' thesis itself — Bitcoin's reliance on alternative energy reveals it isn't actually a hard monetary asset
The 'fixed supply' guarantee — flared-gas mining is allowed to issue extra BTC beyond the 21 million cap as a special exception
The 'decentralization' claim — Bitcoin is now centralized in a few oil-producing nations due to energy economics in 2024
questions.context: Crusoe Energy, Marathon, and others mine Bitcoin from oil-well flare gas — burning the methane productively rather than venting it (worse for climate) or flaring it (mostly wasted). Hydro miners in Sichuan, Texas wind producers, and others demonstrate the same pattern. Bitcoin mining acts as a buyer of last resort for stranded energy.
